lanes.summary: HEAD is 1d8868a26ce930f478f98e64060c06b1d1a2c1f4, the same commit the brief names, so there are no engine diffs. The engine is small (packages/engine/src, about 1,240 lines of pure TS). It is fully deterministic once a deal RNG is injected: applyMove has no randomness, and the 1v1 draw pops from the end of a boneyard array whose order is fixed at the deal. Every rule in the brief matches the code, with three refinements the build prompt must state. (1) Only the mid-round bonuses (pase corrido, pase de salida) are capped, and the cap is strict: they pay only if score+25 < target. Capicua is part of the round win and can end the game. (2) Boneyard pips never score in 1v1. (3) After a 1v1 draw that finds a fit, the only legal tile is the last tile drawn, so the next play is forced except for the choice of end. A parity argument, confirmed on 7,403 tranques in 6,000 seeded games, shows a tranque always has equal ends and all 7 tiles of that suit on the board. The lock test is therefore an O(1) check on a 28-bit board mask. The engine must not copy the legacy saved-game branches: lock on draw or pass, two sides past the target, tranque payloads without winnerSeat, the duplicate pass counter, and the salida sent as a 'veinticinco' callout. Today every client and the anon key receive the full game_state: all four hands plus the ordered boneyard (RLS 'games: public read' using (true)), and no per-round deal is stored anywhere. So the engine API must take only the acting player's information set, and post-game analysis needs a new deal log. Measured on one core of an Apple M1 under Node 18.20.8, the TS reducer runs about 0.30M (2v2) to 0.36M (1v1) applyMove calls per second. A throwaway allocation-free bitmask playout runs about 33.6M plies per second (2v2, no bonuses), about 100x faster. Information sets in 2v2 run from 399,072,960 consistent deals at a free lead to a median under 10^4 once 13 or more tiles are down. Late-round exact enumeration is cheap. Early-round decisions need sampling. The invariant fuzz suite (assertTransition) and flow.endgame's rulesIntents are independent oracles that can be reused for differential testing of a faster engine. The repo has no plan for bots, AI or analysis. The store listing says the opposite: 'there are no computer opponents'.

findings.topic: a. Complete rule list (Capi spec)
findings.claim: Numbered rule list the new engine must reproduce exactly.
findings.detail: SETUP. (1) Double-six set, 28 tiles, enumerated a=0..6, b=a..6 (reducer.ts:27-35). (2) Fisher-Yates shuffle with injected rng; default rng is the CSPRNG (reducer.ts:39-58). (3) Seats: 2v2 = n,e,s,w; 1v1 = n,s (types.ts:112-114). Deal 7 tiles to each seat in seat order from the shuffled array; the rest is the boneyard: 14 in 1v1, 0 in 2v2 (reducer.ts:120-133). Teams: 2v2 n/s = team 0, e/w = team 1; 1v1 n = 0, s = 1 (types.ts:116-119). OPENER. (4) Round 1: the highest double across all hands opens. Seats are scanned in order with a strict '>' compare, so in 2v2 it is always the 6-6. If no hand holds a double (possible only in 1v1), the highest pip-sum tile opens. Ties go to the earlier seat in order (n before s), then to the first such tile in hand order. The tile is removed from the hand and placed automatically, as oriented in the hand (reducer.ts:90-109, 135-163, 174). (5) After the round-1 placement: currentTurn = the seat after the opener, lastPlayedBy = opener, starterThisRound = opener, pass counters = 0 (reducer.ts:176-184). The auto tile counts as the opener's play for both bonuses. (6) Later rounds: the board is empty and the previous round's winner seat leads with any tile. The winner is the player who went out (domino or capicua) or the tranque's winnerSeat. lastPlayedBy = null, roundIndex+1, scores carried over, fresh deal (reducer.ts:482-487, 520-564). startNewRound is a no-op unless phase === 'round_over' (reducer.ts:531). TURN ORDER. (7) 2v2: n->e->s->w->n; 1v1: n<->s (types.ts:103-110). 'The player to the right' = the next seat. LEGAL MOVES. (8) Only in phase 'playing', and only the seat on turn (validate.ts:58-63). (9) Play needs a tile in hand (either orientation) and end in {left, right} (validate.ts:67-81). (10) Empty board: any tile on either end, and the end is irrelevant; the tile is placed as oriented in the intent (validate.ts:82-84, reducer.ts:78). (11) Non-empty board: the tile must contain the pip of the chosen end (validate.ts:85-91). The new open end is the tile's other pip (reducer.ts:79-87). A double d-d fits only an end showing d. With ends L!=R, the tile L-R fits both ends and gives different results: on the left the ends become R|R, on the right L|L. With L==R, both ends give the same position. (12) You must play if you can: pass and draw are rejected while any tile fits (validate.ts:101-103, 107-110). DRAW (1v1 only). (13) Draw is legal only in 1v1, only with no legal play, and only with a non-empty boneyard (validate.ts:94-105). (14) One draw action pops tiles from the END of the boneyard array into the hand and stops right after the first tile that fits, or when the boneyard is empty (reducer.ts:385-394). The turn stays with the drawer. Pass counters are unchanged. A draw never scores (reducer.ts:396-405). (15) After a draw that found a fit, the only playable tile in hand is the last tile drawn, so the next play is forced except for the choice of end (inference from rules 12-14). PASS. (16) A pass is legal only with no legal play, and in 1v1 only once the boneyard is empty (validate.ts:107-115). It advances the turn and increments both pass counters (reducer.ts:408-414, 460-470). ROUND END. (17) Domino: a play that empties the hand ends the round. This is checked before the lock, so going out on the locking tile is a domino (reducer.ts:306-316). Points = the pips in every hand, partner included; boneyard pips are not counted (scoring.ts:35-43). (18) Capicua: on a domino, +25 if the closing tile fits both ends as they were before it was placed (reducer.ts:236-240, scoring.ts:91-98). 3-5 on 3|5 counts. 5-6 on 5|5 counts. 2-2 on 2|2 counts. 2-2 on 2|5 does not. It never applies on an empty board or a tranque. (19) Tranque: after a play that does not empty the hand, the round ends if no tile outside the board (hands and boneyard) fits either end (reducer.ts:318-322, validate.ts:45-51). Blocker = the placer. Rival = the next seat, always an opponent. Compare each player's own hand pips: fewer wins for that player's side. On equal pips, starterThisRound (la mano) wins, even when he is neither of the two. Points = the pips in all hands; boneyard pips are not counted (scoring.ts:63-82). (20) In 1v1 a lock can happen with tiles still in the boneyard (reducer.ts:320; test reducer.test.ts:314). SCORING AND GAME END. (21) Only the round-winning side scores the round (reducer.ts:190-198). If its score reaches the target, phase = 'finished' and winnerTeam is set; otherwise phase = 'round_over' (reducer.ts:206-218, normal path). The target defaults to 100, the engine accepts any number, and the app offers 100 or 200 (reducer.ts:119). (22) Capicua is part of the round score, is not capped, and can win the game (test reducer.test.ts:1537). MID-ROUND BONUSES (2v2 only). (23) Pase corrido: a pass is the 3rd since the last play, the next seat is lastPlayedBy, and lastPlayedBy != null. Then +25 to lastPlayedBy's team, the round continues, and that player must play next. It can repeat in a round (reducer.ts:408-458). In 1v1 the threshold is Infinity (reducer.ts:413). (24) Pase de salida: on a play that does not end the round, if the board held only the opening tile, lastPlayedBy === starterThisRound, passesSinceLastPlay === 1, and the player is the opener's partner, then +25 to the opener's team (reducer.ts:334-373). It applies every round, including the auto 6-6. The partner's pass cancels it. A 4th pass is then a pase corrido and pays 25 once. (25) Cap: either mid-round bonus is paid only if scores[team] + 25 < target, a strict compare, so a bonus never reaches the target. Otherwise the action is a plain move with no callout (reducer.ts:349, 431). (26) Bonuses stack with later round points in the same column (test reducer.test.ts:2021). (27) The next round's leader is the individual round winner (rule 6), not the team. (28) Forfeit is an app rule, not a game rule. In live mode, 120,000 ms of silence on turn lets the other side claim the game; turn_based games never forfeit (forfeit.ts:9, 42-78).
findings.implication: The prompt should give this list verbatim as the Capi rule spec, with the note that the engine must reproduce it and never 'correct' it. Rules 15, 17 (no boneyard pips), 19-20 and 22 (capicua is not capped) are the points most likely to be got wrong.

findings.topic: a. Tranque parity theorem
findings.claim: A tranque always has equal open ends X|X with all 7 tiles of suit X on the board. So the lock depends only on the board: locked iff L==R and popcount(board & suit[L]) == 7.
findings.detail: Proof: Capi chains are linear (no spinner; doubles sit inline, reducer.ts:72-88). If all 7 tiles of suit X are on the board, they carry 8 X-halves (the double counts twice). Every internal junction uses 2 X-halves, so the number of ends showing X is even. A lock with L!=R would need all 7 L-tiles on the board while L shows at only one end, which is impossible. Since every tile is either on the board or outside it, 'no outside tile fits' is the same as 'every tile of the end suit is on the board'. The boneyard part of isBoardLocked (validate.ts:49) is therefore redundant. Checked empirically: 7,403 of 7,403 tranques in 6,000 seeded random games (3,000 1v1 + 3,000 2v2) had equal ends and a full suit on the board. A board-only test agreed with isBoardLocked on all 779,804 post-move states.
sources: docs/research/rules-2026-09/README.md:27 (sources describe the lock as the seventh tile of a suit with both ends showing it)
findings.implication: The fast engine can detect the tranque with one AND and compare per play. The lock is public, so 'the round continues' reveals nothing about hands.

findings.topic: b. Legacy compatibility paths not to reproduce
findings.claim: The engine has saved-game and old-client branches that a new search engine should drop. They cannot be reached from a fresh deal under current rules.
findings.detail: (1) Lock resolved on a draw or pass, with blocker = lastPlayedBy ?? previous seat (reducer.ts:377-383). It exists for games saved before the lock-at-placement rule; a live board is never locked (fuzz invariant at invariants.fuzz.test.ts:187-192). Tests: reducer.test.ts:203, 895-940, 1468. (2) creditRound's branch for 'other side already at the target' and the two-sides-past-target tie (reducer.ts:200-213). It exists for games saved before the pase corrido cap. Tests: reducer.test.ts:2153-2195. (3) getRoundWinningSeat fallbacks: tranque payloads without winnerSeat, which use the compared seat on the winning side, and payloads without comparison fields, which use the lightest hand on the winning side (reducer.ts:489-515). Test: rules.salida-and-tie.test.ts:446, reducer.test.ts:1640. Also the domino fallback 'lastPlayedBy ?? starterThisRound' (reducer.ts:486). (4) The pase de salida sent as a 'veinticinco' callout with salida: true, so that old app builds show +25 (types.ts:27-28, reducer.ts:338-339, 363). This is a wire concern; a new engine should emit distinct event types (CAPICUA, PASE_CORRIDO, PASE_SALIDA) and let an adapter map them. (5) Two pass counters that always hold the same value: consecutivePasses and passesSinceLastPlay are reset and incremented together at every site (reducer.ts:177-178, 327-328, 409-410, 446-447, 465-466, 555-556). Only consecutivePasses is read by the apps (apps/web/src/hooks/useRealtimeGame.ts:117), and only passesSinceLastPlay by the rules. Keep one. (6) scoreDomino keeps an unused winningTeam parameter 'for API stability' (scoring.ts:30-35). (7) The salida guards for unreachable saved states (rules.salida-and-tie.test.ts:250-261, 292-349 say 'Not reachable in live play'). With a closed state machine these become debug assertions. (8) App and session fields mixed into the rules state: mode, theme, players, rematchGameId, lastMoveAt, forfeit, and lastCallout/lastCalloutPayload as UI banners (types.ts:59-87). (9) Wire validation inside the rules path: isTile and the bogus-end checks (validate.ts:13-20, 77-81). These belong at the API boundary, not in the hot loop.
findings.implication: The prompt should say: model only reachable states from a fresh deal, keep one pass counter, emit typed bonus events, keep UI and session fields out of the search state, and validate wire input outside the hot path. Saved-game compatibility stays in the existing Capi reducer, which remains the live referee.

findings.topic: c. Information model: what each public action reveals
findings.claim: Certain deductions per action. Hand sizes, boneyard count, board, scores, the opener and the full action history are public.
findings.detail: PUBLIC STATE: the board with orientation, each hand's size, the boneyard count (1v1), scores, the target, starterThisRound, lastPlayedBy and the pass count. In 2v2, hand sizes follow directly from the play count. ROUND-1 AUTO OPENING: 2v2 reveals only who held the 6-6 (always placed). 1v1: if the opener placed double d, no hand holds a double above d, so every double above d is in the boneyard. If no double was placed, all 7 doubles are in the boneyard and the other hand holds no tile with a higher pip sum; with equal sums the seat-order tie-break applies (reducer.ts:135-159). LEAD on an empty board (round 2+): reveals the tile only, since the leader has free choice. PLAY ON AN END: reveals the tile. Nothing else is certain, because any legal tile may be played. CHOOSING AN END when the tile fits both: nothing certain, only a strategic signal. PASS IN 2v2: certain that the passer holds no tile containing L or R. Hands never grow in 2v2, so this void lasts for the rest of the round. PASS IN 1v1 (boneyard empty): the same void, and it also lasts for the round, because no more draws are possible. DRAW IN 1v1 of k tiles (k is public as hand delta = boneyard delta): (i) the drawer held no L or R tile before drawing. (ii) The first k-1 tiles drawn contain neither L nor R. (iii) If a fit was found, the k-th tile fits and is played next, forced, so it becomes public. If the boneyard ran out with no fit, the drawer passes next and all k tiles are void of L and R. Voids in 1v1 are time-stamped. They bind the tiles held at that moment, not tiles drawn later, so a 1v1 observer must track acquisition batches: initial hand, then each draw's non-fitting tiles, each batch constrained by the ends at every later draw or pass while it is held. PASE CORRIDO: three 2v2 voids at once. ROUND END: the payload reveals both sides' pip totals, and for a tranque the blocker's and rival's pips (reducer.ts:229-234, 256-266). TRANQUE ITSELF: a function of the board alone (parity finding), so it adds no hand information.
sources: packages/engine/__tests__/invariants.fuzz.test.ts:288-300 (draw stops at a playable tile or an empty boneyard)
findings.implication: The engine needs an Observation/InfoSet type: own hand, public board and history, hand sizes, boneyard count, per-seat void constraints (2v2: suit sets; 1v1: time-stamped batch constraints) and the 1v1 round-1 opening deductions. The world sampler must respect all of these exactly. The draw should be modeled as a chance node over an unordered boneyard.

findings.topic: c. What the Capi server sends clients today
findings.claim: Every client, and anyone holding the public anon key, receives the full game_state: all four hands and the boneyard in draw order. Hidden information is hidden only by the UI.
findings.detail: GET /api/games/[id] returns select('*') on games, including game_state (apps/web/src/app/api/games/[id]/route.ts:15-19, 47). POST /move returns the full newState to the mover (move/route.ts:78-90, 107-113). The mover rebroadcasts it to the table on the chat channel (apps/web/src/hooks/useRealtimeGame.ts:741-750). Every client subscribes to postgres_changes UPDATE on games and applies payload.new.game_state (useRealtimeGame.ts:371-397; mobile mirror apps/mobile/hooks/useRealtimeGame.ts:403-413). RLS allows anyone to read games ('games: public read' using (true), supabase/migrations/001_initial.sql:22-24). Migration 005 keeps reads open on purpose (005_lock_direct_writes.sql:15-17). The UI picks which hands to draw face up (apps/web/src/app/game/[id]/page.tsx:907-928). Because the boneyard array is ordered and draws pop from its end (reducer.ts:390-391), a 1v1 client can see exactly which tiles it would draw. The moves table logs only the intent and callout (move/route.ts:94-104; 001_initial.sql:58-68), with no deal and no drawn tiles. game_state is overwritten on every move and every new round. No per-round deal is persisted, so a finished game cannot be replayed from stored data today.
findings.implication: The engine API must accept only the acting player's information set, never GameState, so that a bot cannot read hidden tiles even when they are in memory, and analysis can say what was best given what the player knew. Post-game analysis needs a new per-round record: the deal (hands, boneyard order, opener) plus the ordered action list. With that record, replay through the deterministic reducer is exact. Masking game_state per seat is a separate app change the owner should know about.

findings.topic: d. State representation and branching
findings.claim: 28 tiles fit in a 28-bit mask, and the lock test is O(1). Distinct legal plays per turn are at most 8 in 2v2 and at most 12 in 1v1.
findings.detail: Tile index = Capi's ALL_TILES order (a=0..6, b=a..6, reducer.ts:27-35). suit[p] = 7-bit-set mask of the tiles containing p. Move generation = hand & (suit[L] | suit[R]). Distinct-move bound, after merging left and right when L==R and on an empty board: on an empty board, hand size = 7, so 7 moves (14 raw (tile, end) pairs, because validate.ts:82-84 accepts either end). With L!=R, a 1-tile board leaves at most 12 outside tiles containing L or R; a board of 2 or more tiles uses two of the 13, leaving 11 outside, plus 1 for the L-R tile played two ways, so at most 12. With L==R, at most 6. In 2v2 the hand is at most 7, so at most 8. Measured with a random policy, 3,000 games per format to 100: max distinct plays 12 in 1v1 and 8 in 2v2. Max raw (tile, end) pairs was 12 in both. Mean distinct plays when a play exists: 2.16 (1v1) and 2.40 (2v2). Max hand size: 21 in theory in 1v1 (7 + 14); 20 observed. Max tiles in one draw: 14 observed (the whole boneyard). Mean tiles per draw: 2.13. Pip values enter the scoring, so pip relabeling gives no symmetry; only the left/right mirror of the board is a symmetry.
findings.implication: Fixed move buffers of 12 (1v1) and 8 (2v2) entries, plus 7 on an empty board, are enough. Merge symmetric moves (L==R, empty board) before search, but keep the user-facing end choice for the UI.

findings.topic: d. Plies per round
findings.claim: Hard bounds: 2v2 at most 25 plays and at most 97 decisions per round. 1v1 at most 27 plays, 14 draws and 26 passes (67 decisions). Observed max is about 44, mean about 23-25.
findings.detail: 2v2: the round ends when the first player goes out. At that moment the others have played at most 6 each, so at most 7+6+6+6 = 25 tiles are on the board (the round-1 auto tile counts but is not a decision). At most 3 passes come between two plays, because a 4th would be a locked board, which ends the round at placement (invariant at invariants.fuzz.test.ts:191-192). So decisions <= 25 + 3*24 = 97. 1v1: at most 27 tiles placed (the loser keeps at least 1). Each draw takes at least 1 tile, so at most 14 draws. Passes happen only with an empty boneyard and never twice in a row, so at most 26. Bound: 67. Measured with a random policy over 3,000 games each to target 100: 1v1 mean 22.46 and max 44 applyMove calls per round, 7.14 rounds per game, 3.74 draws per round; 2v2 mean 25.42 and max 42 calls per round, 3.25 passes per round, 3.93 rounds per game. Ending mix (random policy): 1v1 domino 68.4%, capicua 12.3%, tranque 19.4% of 21,419 rounds; 2v2 domino 55.9%, capicua 17.8%, tranque 26.3% of 11,787 rounds.
findings.implication: A round is a shallow tree, at most about 25 plays deep. Full-depth search per sampled world is feasible, so the prompt can require exact perfect-information solves inside a determinization or ISMCTS loop, with a 128-ply history cap as a safe bound.

findings.topic: d. Deals and opponent-hand completions
findings.claim: 2v2 has 472,518,347,558,400 deals and 1v1 has 137,680,171,200. Consistent completions for the acting player go from 399,072,960 (2v2 free lead) to a median under 10^4 by mid-round, and 1v1 never exceeds 116,280.
findings.detail: Formulas: 2v2 deals = 28!/(7!)^4 = 472,518,347,558,400. 1v1 deals = 28!/(7!*7!*14!) = C(28,7)*C(21,7) = 137,680,171,200 (unordered boneyard; Capi also stores the order, which is equivalent in distribution). Own hands: C(28,7) = 1,184,040. 2v2 from one seat: free lead 21!/(7!)^3 = 399,072,960; round 1 for a non-opener (6-6 down, opener holds 6) 20!/(6!7!7!) = 133,024,320; when each other seat holds k tiles, (3k)!/(k!)^3 = 17,153,136 / 756,756 / 34,650 / 1,680 / 90 / 6 for k = 6..1. 1v1: C(U,h) where U = opponent hand + boneyard: deal C(21,7) = 116,280; round 1 non-opener C(20,6) = 38,760; for example C(19,5) = 11,628, C(14,6) = 3,003, C(8,4) = 70. Measured in 2v2 (300 random games, 31,000+ decisions) as the exact void-constrained count of consistent deals (DP over tiles, voids from passes), median by board size: 0 tiles 399,072,960; 4 tiles 17,153,136; 8 tiles 756,756; 12 tiles 34,650; 13 tiles 7,350 (11,550 unconstrained); 16 tiles 560 (1,680); 20 tiles 22 (60); the minimum reaches 1 from 17 tiles on. Pass voids cut the count 2-3x from mid-round and up to about 300x early in some deals (board 1: min 411,840 vs 133,024,320).
findings.implication: The engine can enumerate all consistent worlds exactly in 1v1 (at most 116,280 hands, times boneyard chance) and in 2v2 from about 13 tiles on the board (median under 10^4). Early 2v2 decisions need sampling, ideally weighted by an opponent model, since uniform sampling ignores what voluntary plays signal.

findings.topic: e. Suitability of the TS reducer for search
findings.claim: The reducer is pure and deterministic but allocation-heavy, with no make/unmake. It suits use as a reference oracle, not as the search core.
findings.detail: Per play, applyMove: validateMove (linear tileInHand); removeTileFromHand, which allocates a new array (two slices and a spread, reducer.ts:66-70); placeTileOnBoard, an O(board) copy of the whole board array plus a new tuple (reducer.ts:72-88); two full GameState object spreads of about 22 keys each plus a new hands object (reducer.ts:299-304, 324-332); isBoardLocked, which flattens all hands and the boneyard into a new array on every play (validate.ts:47-51). A pass spreads the state and runs hasLegalPlay and isBoardLocked. A draw copies the boneyard and hand arrays and calls hasLegalPlay once per drawn tile. A round end computes teamPips, which iterates all hands again, and builds payload objects. There is no undo, no exported move generator (each test writes its own legalPlays), no hash or Zobrist key, and tiles are [a, b] tuples whose orientation matters. Determinism: rng is injectable for the deal (reducer.ts:111-121), applyMove has no randomness, and the fuzz suite proves no in-place mutation with deepFreeze (invariants.fuzz.test.ts:49-55, 374) and survives a JSON round trip (:387). Measured, single thread, Apple M1 (8 cores, 8 GB), Node v18.20.8, esbuild bundle of packages/engine/src at 1d8868a, random legal policy, target 100, 3,000 games after a 200-game warm-up: 1v1 2,253 games/s, 16,084 rounds/s, 361,226 applyMove calls/s; 2v2 2,983 games/s, 11,721 rounds/s, 297,999 applyMove calls/s (the harness's move generation is included). For comparison, a throwaway allocation-free bitmask 2v2 playout (play, pass, domino and tranque detection; no bonuses or scoring) on the same machine ran 33,559,544 plies/s and 1,351,034 rounds/s over 2,000,000 rounds: about 110x more plies per second. It is not a like-for-like engine.
findings.implication: The prompt should require a new core with bitmask state, in-place make/unmake or cheap value copies, a move generator, and a hash key. Keep the existing reducer as the reference referee and set a throughput target. A first-pass JS bitmask core already reaches about 30M plies/s per core on an M1, so a Rust or C++ core (WASM for clients) should beat that.

findings.topic: e. Fuzz and flow suites as differential oracles
findings.claim: invariants.fuzz.test.ts and flow.endgame.test.ts recompute the rules independently of the engine helpers. They can check a faster engine transition by transition.
findings.detail: assertTransition(prev, next, seat, intent, label) (invariants.fuzz.test.ts:140-336) checks: conservation of the 28 tiles, a valid chain, monotone integer scores, the phase machine and the target, a live board never locked, fewer than 4 consecutive passes, play effects, salida shape and payment, domino and capicua points recomputed, tranque blocker, rival and winnerSeat recomputed, all-hands points, draw stop conditions, and pase corrido payment and cap. expectedNextStarter (:339-345) checks who leads next. It also counts how often each rule path is reached, and asserts that every path was reached (:421-473), including 4 whole-suit seeds (59313, 83322, 282144, 645301) for the rare salida-cancel-then-corrido path. flow.endgame.test.ts:84-95 rulesIntents is an independent legal-move oracle (acceptedIntents must equal rulesIntents), and it holds four baseline policies: random, greedy-heavy, passive-light, and blocker, which peeks at the next hand (:130-160). Limits: the fuzz policies play only 'right' on an empty board (invariants.fuzz.test.ts:60-62), so left-lead orientation is never exercised. Bit-identical comparison also needs the same deal: shuffle(ALL_TILES, rng) with mulberry32 and the slice order (reducer.ts:51-58, 121-133), or a harness that injects Capi's deal into the new engine. Boneyard order matters because draws pop from the end.
findings.implication: The prompt should require a differential harness. Seeded deals go into both engines (or Capi's deal is injected into the new one), the same intent sequence is played, and after every move the canonical states are compared (hand sets, board, boneyard order, scores, turn, phase, event type) and assertTransition is run on the new engine's output mapped to GameState. Add left-end leads, which the existing fuzz never generates.

findings.topic: f. Where Capi's rules differ from other Dominican tables (configurable)
findings.claim: Several Capi rules are owner choices among real variants. Most are cheap to make into config flags.
findings.detail: From the research README and synthesis (sources there; not Capi code): (1) Rule set: regla general (FID, FEMUNDO) has no bonuses at all; Capi plays patio (README:11-19). (2) Capicua with a double: Capi counts it when both ends show the number (owner, 2026-09-28). Wikipedia's DR section and DR1 exclude doubles. FichaFlow also excludes 5-6 on 5|5 (README:23, 88-96). DR1 also voids a capicua 'with a blank', meaning unclear (synthesis capicua variants). (3) Bonus values: 25 (Capi), 30 at some tables, DR1's salida of 10 at 200/250; some groups double the hand instead (README:23-25, 64). (4) Can a bonus win the game: no Dominican source. Capi uses a strict cap below the target, matching Boarden (README:26, 41-42). (5) Pase de salida: not universal (La Guáyiga 2025 and the DR1 forum omit it). When all three pass, Capi pays 25 once while two apps pay both (README:60-65). (6) Pase corrido: Santiago 2019 pays 0, and La Guáyiga's '+30 al equipo contrario' is ambiguous (synthesis pases variants). (7) Tranque comparison: patio blocker vs right (Capi), pair totals (regla general), or 'con todo el mundo' (README:27; synthesis tranque). (8) Tranque tie: opener wins (Capi; DR1), a draw with no points (Santiago 2019, FID), or blocker wins (FichaFlow) (README:67). (9) Tranque points: all hands (Capi) vs opponents only (DR1 wording) vs the difference. Still open for the owner (README:106-107). (10) Domino points: all hands including the partner (Capi; patio, FID) vs opponents only (Dominican press regla general; DR1 at 200/250) (README:28). (11) Next opener: the individual winner (Capi) vs either partner of the winning team vs a rotating salida (tournaments, FID) (synthesis setup-turns). (12) 1v1: no Dominican source on the highest-double or highest-tile fallback, the bonuses in 1v1, boneyard pips, or drawing; Wikipedia also lists a 10-tiles-each, no-draw 1v1 (synthesis setup-turns, scoring). (13) Targets 100 or 200 (also 150, 250, 300, 500). (14) Redeal on 5 or 7 doubles in some tournaments; Capi never redeals.
sources: docs/research/rules-2026-09/synthesis.json (topics capicua, pases, tranque, scoring, setup-turns, variants: 'variants' and 'openQuestions' fields)
findings.implication: The prompt should define a RulesConfig whose default equals Capi exactly and whose cheap flags are: capicuaDoubleCounts, capicuaEqualEndsNonDouble, bonus values (capicua, corrido, salida), bonusesEnabled (general vs patio), bonusCanReachTarget, salidaEnabled, salidaAndCorridoBothPay, tranqueMode (blockerVsRight or pairTotals), tranqueTie (opener, blocker or noPoints), pointsCountPartner (domino and tranque separately), nextLeader (winnerSeat, winningTeam or rotate), targetScore. 1v1 variants such as 10 tiles with no draw are a stretch goal. Every flag needs a differential test against Capi at its default value.

findings.topic: 4. Existing plans for bots, AI, analysis
findings.claim: No existing plan for bots, AI, a computer opponent or post-game analysis was found in docs/ideas-after-1.1.md or the roadmap memory. The store listing positions Capi as having no computer opponents.
findings.detail: docs/ideas-after-1.1.md has five items (tile backs, Smart App Banner, store preview, 100/200 in iMessage, voice notes; lines 5-15) and no bot or AI line. The project_capi_post_1_0_roadmap.md memory (37 lines) has no bot, AI or analysis plan. Related lines: docs/store-listing.md:25 says 'Every seat is a real person (there are no computer opponents), so bring your crew.' The Spanish copy says the same at :71, and both repeat at :116 and :157. docs/store-listing.md:4 positions Capi against competitors that are 'generic block dominoes apps with bots'. 'Bots' elsewhere means scripted test players driven through the API (project_capi_dev_loop_gotchas.md:27 'Test bots: POST /api/games with {"mode":"live"}...'; docs/polish-pass-1.1-2026-09-26.md:158-159; docs/m5-submission-checklist.md:159).
findings.implication: The prompt should treat the engine as a new, standalone package (for example packages/solver, or a separate repo) that does not change live play. Shipping bots later contradicts the current store copy, so that is an owner decision to flag.

open_questions: Tranque points: all hands (current spec) or opponents only? The research README lists this as open for the owner (docs/research/rules-2026-09/README.md:106-107). The engine should keep it as a flag defaulting to all hands.

Must the new engine reproduce Capi's deal bit for bit (mulberry32 seed -> shuffle(ALL_TILES) -> slice order, boneyard popped from the end) so the existing seeds replay identically? The alternative is a harness that injects Capi's deal into the new engine. The second option is simpler and keeps the new engine's RNG free.

The 1v1 round-1 tie-breaks with no double held (earlier seat wins equal pip sums, then hand order, reducer.ts:146-159) are code artifacts with no rule source. Should the engine reproduce them exactly? It must for differential parity.

What should the engine maximize: P(win game) at the current score and target (bonus cap and target edge included), or expected round points? Win probability needs a game-level equity model on top of the round search.

Post-game analysis needs a per-round deal log, which Capi does not store today (game_state is overwritten; the moves table has intents only). The owner must decide where to store it, given that the repo is public and reads of games are public.

Should game_state be masked per seat on the server before bots ship? Today all hands and the boneyard order are readable by any client and by the anon key. This is not an engine change, but it affects how fair bots and analysis can claim to be.
The store listing promises 'no computer opponents' (docs/store-listing.md:25). Adding Capi bots needs an owner decision and a copy change.

lanes.summary: The first strong engine for both modes should be PIMC (determinization plus an exact perfect-information solve). PIMC is the proven state of the art for bridge card play (GIB) and Skat (Kermit), and it is cheap for Dominican dominoes. My scratch benchmark (C, Apple M1, one core, simplified Capi-like scoring, checked against naive minimax on 550 positions with 0 mismatches) solves a full 2v2 deal exactly from the opening in a median 7.7 ms (1.67e5 nodes); with 21 tiles left in hands the median is 0.35 ms. 2v2 reveals hidden information faster than Skat: one seat's information set falls from 10^7.5 consistent deals at its first turn to 10^2.3 at its fifth, about 4.1 halvings per own turn (df about 0.80 under Long et al.'s model, against about 0.6 for Skat). Long et al.'s synthetic results put that region where PIMC is strong, but this mapping is an analogy, not a proof. In a pilot (500 duplicate pairs, about 0.3 s per round), PIMC with 20 worlds beat a heaviest-tile bot by +21.3 points/round (SE 1.1). An omniscient team beat PIMC by +49.2 points/round (SE 0.9), so better inference has a large upper bound on its value. The main structural weakness of PIMC in 2v2 is not raw search. In every sampled world the partner is omniscient, so PIMC gives zero value to signaling the partner or hiding information (Frank and Basin; Russell and Norvig via Cowling 2012). Partner-aware inference and search must therefore come after the baseline. Full-game CFR methods (DeepStack, Libratus, Pluribus, ReBeL, Student of Games) do not fit at the opening: a player has C(28,7)=1,184,040 possible private hands, 893 times heads-up hold'em's 1,326, and 2v2 is an adversarial team game where two-player zero-sum guarantees do not hold. They become useful for late, small endgames and as a research tier. Measurement needs large samples. One round's point margin has SD 28 to 45 points; in my tests duplicate replay cut the games needed only 1.1 to 1.65 times, and simple deal-feature control variates cut them 1.05 times. So the build needs duplicate pairs, AIVAT-style control variates from the engine's own value function, and SPRT over thousands of rounds. Recommended ladder, each step proven before the next: (0) a bitboard rules core proven by perft-style line counts, invariants, and differential fuzzing against packages/engine (target 0 mismatches over 1e6 or more random rounds); (1) random, greedy, and rule bots plus a duplicate match harness with SPRT; (2) an exact alpha-beta+TT perfect-information solver, checked against naive minimax and timed; (3) PIMC with exact uniform consistent-world sampling and match-equity leaf utility, proven by duplicate SPRT against the baselines and by reporting its gap to the omniscient bound; (4) policy-based inference (Rebstock et al.) with learned partner and opponent models, proven by the true-state sampling ratio on held-out Capi games plus SPRT; (5) exact endgames by enumerating every consistent world once the count is small (and alpha-mu or small CFR for 1v1), proven by measuring PIMC endgame error against the exact solution; (6) fixes for strategy fusion and for modeling the partner (ISMCTS with partially observable moves for 1v1 draws, EPIMC, and SPARTA-style search with a partner blueprint), proven by SPRT and by cross-play with human-model partners; (7) small information-set value and policy nets trained on search labels, then self-play with a perfect-information critic (PerfectDou-style), proven by SPRT and by Brier-score calibration of the reported win probability; (8) a research tier of ReBeL/SoG-style 1v1 late-game solving and team-CFR (TB-DAG) for 2v2 endgames, proven by exploitability on small endgames. To show the engine beats elite humans, use NooK-style duplicate comparison: humans and the engine play the same deals against the same fixed bot opponents.

findings.topic: PIMC (determinization + perfect-information solve): what it is and evidence
findings.claim: PIMC samples full deals that agree with the player's information, solves each one exactly as a perfect-information game, and plays the move with the best average. It is the documented state of the art for bridge card play and Skat, and is the right first strong engine for both Capi modes.
sources: Ginsberg, GIB: Imperfect Information in a Computationally Challenging Game, JAIR 14:303-358, 2001, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.0669
Buro, Long, Furtak, Sturtevant, Improving State Evaluation, Inference, and Search in Trick-Based Card Games, IJCAI 2009, https://cs.du.edu/~sturtevant/papers/skat.pdf
Cazenave and Ventos, The alpha-mu Search Algorithm for the Game of Bridge, 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.07960 (states 'The best Bridge and Skat programs use PIMC')
findings.implication: The build prompt should make PIMC with an exact solver at the leaves the first strong baseline for 1v1 and 2v2, and the reference that later techniques must beat by SPRT.
findings.detail: GIB: double-dummy solver using partition search; Monte Carlo over 50 sampled deals (100 with extra time). GIB solved 64.4% of Bridge Master problems given extra time, 100 deals, and hand-written bid explanations. Ginsberg puts the club-to-expert gap at about 1.5 IMPs/deal and the SD at about 5.5 IMPs/deal. His later achievable-sets version beat the Monte Carlo version by only about 0.1 IMPs/deal. Kermit (Skat): PIMC with alpha-beta, TT, and move ordering (fastest-cut-first cut search effort by about 40%), plus inference; it was the first expert-level Skat program. Failure modes: strategy fusion, non-locality, and no information-gathering or hiding plays (see separate finding). Cost: low once an exact solver exists. Fit: (a) 1v1 good, but the boneyard draw order must also be sampled, which adds clairvoyance about draws; (b) 2v2 very good on cost and disambiguation, but blind to partner signaling.

findings.topic: Own measurement: exact perfect-information solver cost for dominoes
findings.claim: An exact, score-valued alpha-beta+TT solve of a full 2v2 deal takes milliseconds on one M1 core, so PIMC can afford hundreds of worlds per move in 2v2. 1v1 with a determinized draw order is cheaper at the median but has a heavy tail.
sources: Own scratch benchmark: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-Adelson-Desktop-personal/8fffa044-f991-4add-a6d7-951296d03a0d/scratchpad/research/algorithms/bench/solve.c (200 deals), stage.c (300 positions per stage), test.c and test17.c (cross-check vs naive minimax)
findings.implication: Use an exact solver as the PIMC leaf in 2v2 from move one; no perfect-information value net is needed for 2v2. In 1v1, cap nodes per world and fall back to a depth-limited evaluation for the rare explosive draw lines.
findings.detail: Rules simplified and not the Capi engine: first round only, 6-6 opener; domino = all pips in all hands; capicua +25; tranque decided by blocker vs next player, ties to la mano; pase corrido and pase de salida +25, paid immediately; no match target. TT key = four 28-bit hand masks + canonical (lo, hi) ends + mover + pass count. This key is exact under perfect information. 2v2, 200 random deals, uncontended M1 core, cc -O2: exact root value median 1.67e5 nodes, 7.7 ms; p90 2.93e5 nodes, 15 ms; max 6.39e5 nodes, 44 ms. Exact values of all first moves: median 8.4 ms. Whole reachable state space per deal: median 2.18e6 states (max 5.72e6); complete play lines per deal: median 6.32e6 (max 2.63e7). Cost by stage (300 random-play positions each, measured while 4 other processes ran): median solve 12.2 ms at 27 tiles left in hands, 1.76 ms at 24, 0.345 ms at 21, 0.062 ms at 18, 0.015 ms at 15, 0.004 ms at 12. 1v1, 7/7 hands with a fixed 14-tile draw order, 200 deals: median 7,800 nodes, 0.46 ms; p90 1.0e5 nodes, 3.3 ms; max 4.87e7 nodes, 1.09 s. Correctness: alpha-beta+TT equals naive full minimax on 400 positions with 13 tiles left and 150 positions with 17 tiles left, 0 mismatches.

findings.topic: Own measurement: PIMC strength pilot in 2v2
findings.claim: PIMC with 20 worlds beats a heaviest-tile bot by about 21 points/round. A perfect-information (omniscient) team beats that PIMC by about 49 points/round, so hidden information is worth a lot in 2v2 dominoes and inference has a large upper bound on its value.
sources: Own scratch benchmark: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-Adelson-Desktop-personal/8fffa044-f991-4add-a6d7-951296d03a0d/scratchpad/research/algorithms/bench/pimc.c, pimc2.c, results r1.txt, r2.txt, r3.txt, r5.txt
findings.implication: The prompt should demand the same three reference points for every engine version: margin vs a heuristic bot, margin vs the previous version, and the remaining gap to an omniscient team (the upper bound on what better inference can gain).
findings.detail: Duplicate pairs (each deal played twice, teams swap seats). Same simplified rules as the solver finding. Worlds sampled exactly and uniformly under hard pass-void constraints with a DP; every world solved exactly. PIMC20 vs heaviest-tile: +21.33 points/round, 500 pairs, SE 1.09, SD 37.8 per round. Omniscient vs heaviest: +54.32, 500 pairs, SE 0.77. Omniscient vs PIMC20: +49.24, 500 pairs, SE 0.86. PIMC20 vs PIMC5: +3.70, 300 pairs, SE 1.79 (about 2 SE). Speed: about 0.4 s per round for 1000 rounds with two PIMC20 seats, one M1 core under load. A planned PIMC100 self-play null test (expected mean 0) was stopped unfinished and gave no result.

findings.topic: Long, Sturtevant, Buro, Furtak 2010 predictors, and measured disambiguation for 2v2 dominoes
findings.claim: Long et al. define leaf correlation, bias, and disambiguation factor as predictors of PIMC quality. 2v2 dominoes measures df of about 0.80, higher than Skat's 0.6, which their synthetic results associate with strong PIMC play.
sources: Long, Sturtevant, Buro, Furtak, Understanding the Success of Perfect Information Monte Carlo Sampling in Game Tree Search, AAAI 2010, pp. 134-140, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/7562
findings.implication: Have the engine log information-set sizes per turn, which tells the build when exact enumeration replaces sampling. Expect PIMC to be relatively stronger in 2v2 than in 1v1.
findings.detail: Definitions: leaf correlation lc = probability that all sibling terminal nodes have the same payoff; bias b = probability that the game favors one player; df = how fast a player's information set shrinks between that player's turns. Synthetic findings: high lc favors PIMC; df near 1 (0.7 to 0.9) makes PIMC strong. Skat and Hearts measured lc 0.8 to 1.0 and df about 0.6, where PIMC loses about 0.1 points/game vs equilibrium on a [-1, 1] payoff scale. Kuhn poker (lc 0.5, b 0.5, df 0) is the bad case. Own 2v2 measurement counts only hard constraints: own hand, board, hand sizes, and voids from passes. Mean log10 of seat 0's consistent deals by its own turn: 7.53, 6.15, 4.78, 3.48, 2.28, 1.26, 0.71. Mean shrink: 4.06 halvings per own turn (ratio 0.090) with uniform-random play, 4.08 with heaviest-tile play. The df of 0.80 uses my conversion E[k]=df/(1-df) from their halving model. lc as defined is close to 1 by construction in dominoes, because going out ends the round whichever end is used; this is my inference and was not measured. 1v1 has lower df: the 14-tile boneyard stays unknown, giving 116,280 possible opponent hands at the start plus the draw order. 1v1 df was not measured.

findings.topic: Strategy fusion, non-locality, and the partnership blind spot of PIMC
findings.claim: PIMC errs through strategy fusion (it acts as if it could choose differently in worlds it cannot tell apart) and non-locality (it ignores that opponents steer play using their private information). It also never makes information-gathering or information-hiding plays. In 2v2 this means the partner is omniscient in every sampled world, so PIMC gives zero value to signaling the partner.
sources: Frank and Basin, Search in games with incomplete information: a case study using Bridge card play, Artificial Intelligence 100, 1998 (as summarized in Long et al. 2010 and Cowling et al. 2012)

Cowling, Powley, Whitehouse, Information Set Monte Carlo Tree Search, IEEE TCIAIG 4(2):120-143, 2012, https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75048/1/CowlingPowleyWhitehouse2012.pdf (quotes Russell and Norvig, and Ginsberg's GIB remarks)
findings.implication: After the PIMC baseline, the prompt must require a component that models partner and opponents as agents acting on their own information (inference from their plays, and partner-aware search or learned policies). Test 'communicative' plays explicitly, for example duplicate deals where signaling matters.
findings.detail: Applying the partnership consequence to dominoes is my inference: PIMC treats partner and opponents as seeing all hands, so it is paranoid about opponents and overconfident about partner coordination. Frank and Basin's own fix was a heuristic for bridge endgames. Long et al. note PIMC can be exploited by an opponent who models it (Kuhn poker: PIMC as player 2 gets -0.166 vs a best response, where Nash play wins 0.056).

findings.topic: Information Set MCTS (SO-ISMCTS, SO-ISMCTS+POM, MO-ISMCTS)
findings.claim: ISMCTS builds one search tree over information sets, sampling one determinization per iteration. In Dou Di Zhu it tied determinized UCT overall, winning on deals where hidden information matters and losing elsewhere. MO-ISMCTS helps only when moves are partially observable.
sources: Whitehouse, Cowling, Powley, Rollason, Integrating MCTS with Knowledge-Based Methods to Create Engaging Play in a Commercial Mobile Game, AIIDE 2013, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AIIDE/article/view/12679
Sievers and Helmert, A Doppelkopf Player Based on UCT, KI 2015, https://ai.dmi.unibas.ch/papers/sievers-helmert-ki2015.pdf
findings.implication: Use ISMCTS as a step-6 candidate. In 1v1, use the variant that treats draws as partially observable moves. In 2v2 a single SO-ISMCTS tree is enough, because every tile play and pass is public.
findings.detail: Dou Di Zhu, 5000 deals x 75 plays: determinized UCT 43.6%, ISMCTS 42.3%, cheating UCT 56.5%. ISMCTS was better on the 1421 deals where cheating beat determinization. Failure mode: the union of legal moves across worlds inflates branching, which hurt in Dou Di Zhu. In dominoes I expect this to hurt less, because a turn has a few tile-and-end options (inference). SO-ISMCTS assumes opponents know the root player's hidden information and assumes random opponent play on partially observable moves (paper limitations). Commercial evidence: AI Factory Spades, a 2v2 partnership game with more than 2.5 million downloads, used MCTS plus knowledge to cut plays that humans see as partner blunders. Doppelkopf: ensemble UCT over a few fixed card assignments scored about 4.52 vs -1.25 for single UCT (poster, points per game). Cost: moderate. Fit: (a) 1v1 good, since the root player's decisions are not fused across future draws; (b) 2v2 medium unless the partner is modeled.

findings.topic: alpha-mu search (Cazenave and Ventos)
findings.claim: alpha-mu searches over vectors of outcomes per world with Pareto fronts. It fixes strategy fusion and non-locality for the Max side, assuming the opponents have perfect information. It gave small gains over PIMC in bridge at about 13 times the time per move.
sources: Cazenave and Ventos, The alpha-mu Search Algorithm for the Game of Bridge, 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.07960
Cazenave, Legras, Ventos, Optimizing alpha-mu, 2021, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.12639
findings.implication: Offer alpha-mu as an optional 1v1 endgame refinement. Its outcomes must be generalized from win/loss to match-equity values. Do not use it as a 2v2 core.
findings.detail: 3NT declarer play on deals filtered to a 30 to 70% PIMC win rate. 52 cards, 20 worlds: PIMC 60.2% vs alpha-mu M=3 62.0%. 52 cards, 40 worlds: 62.4% vs 63.2%. 36 cards, 20 worlds: 46.4% vs 48.2%. Time per move: 0.096 s (M=1) vs 1.228 s (M=3 with TT and cuts), 18.678 s without them. The 2021 optimizations made it about 3 times faster, and leaf parallelization about 2 times more. Failure modes: binary outcomes only, and opponents are assumed omniscient. Fit: (a) 1v1 medium (endgames); (b) 2v2 poor, because the partner is a separate agent with private information, unlike bridge's declarer, who sees and controls dummy.

findings.topic: Recursive and extended PIMC (IIMC, EPIMC)
findings.claim: IIMC (Furtak and Buro) runs PIMC recursively to reduce strategy fusion and became the state of the art in Skat. EPIMC (Arjonilla, Saffidine, Cazenave, CoG 2024) delays the perfect-information leaf solve to depth d, with d=1 equal to PIMC, and reports gains where strategy fusion matters.
sources: Furtak, Symmetries and Search in Trick-Taking Card Games, PhD thesis, University of Alberta, 2013 (ch. 9 IIMC), https://era.library.ualberta.ca/items/df9f1055-df09-43ed-910b-38da4e9d0792
Solinas, Rebstock, Buro, AAAI 2019 (describes IIMC as Skat state of the art), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.09604
Arjonilla, Saffidine, Cazenave, Perfect Information Monte Carlo with Postponing Reasoning, 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.02380
findings.implication: These are cheap step-6 upgrades on top of PIMC, because the dominoes leaf solver is fast. Each must pass SPRT against plain PIMC.
findings.detail: Cost: nested sampling multiplies solves by roughly worlds^depth, which is affordable in 2v2 after the first trick round, given 0.35 ms per solve at 21 tiles left in hands (own measurement). Fit: (a) 1v1 medium; (b) 2v2 medium. Neither models the partner as non-omniscient.

findings.topic: Inference in Skat (Kermit, Solinas 2019, Rebstock 2019 policy-based inference)
findings.claim: Weighting sampled worlds by how likely the observed actions are under a model of the other players is the largest proven gain on top of PIMC in trick-taking games.
sources: Solinas, Rebstock, Buro, Improving Search with Supervised Learning in Trick-Based Card Games, AAAI 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.09604
Rebstock, Solinas, Buro, Sturtevant, Policy Based Inference in Trick-Taking Card Games, IEEE CoG 2019, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.10911
findings.implication: Step 4 should sample worlds exactly and uniformly under hard constraints, then weight them by the product of modeled action probabilities for each opponent and partner decision (and each pass). Use separate partner and opponent models trained on Capi logs and self-play. Report the true-state sampling ratio (TSSR) on held-out games and SPRT results.
findings.detail: Kermit, 1600 card-play games per pairing (each deal played twice with roles swapped), 60 CPU s per game, 2.5 GHz Xeon: with inference 996 vs 779 points per 36-game series without. Inference by defenders about the soloist helped most, and the Skat defenders are a temporary two-player team. Solinas 2019: a neural net predicting card locations from move history samples worlds better and wins in null and suit games; metric TSSR = p(true state | history) x number of states. Rebstock 2019: policy model gives P(history | state); information sets of up to 2.8e9 states are subsampled; PI beats the earlier method by 2.32, 0.64, and 1.57 tournament points per game across game types. Dominoes specifics (inference): a pass proves the passer holds neither end number, and in 2v2 this void lasts the whole round. My df.c shows exact counting, and hence exact uniform sampling, is a small DP over tiles. 1v1 constraints are tied to draw times (tiles held at that moment), so they need a history-consistent sampler (sequential importance or rejection sampling). Fit: (a) 1v1 high; (b) 2v2 high.

findings.topic: Bridge engines (GIB, Jack, WBridge5, BEN, NooK)
findings.claim: Strong bridge programs combine sampling consistent with bidding and play, a fast double-dummy solver, and (recently) neural networks for bidding. Even mature bots do not interpret partner signals well.
sources: 19th World Computer-Bridge Championship, ICGA Journal 2015 (Jack 10th title, beat WBridge5 165-148), https://content.iospress.com/articles/icga-journal/icg0006
findings.implication: Treat partner-signal modeling as an open problem that needs explicit tests. Use bridge's 'sample consistent with conventions' pattern for dominoes partner inference.
findings.detail: Jack and WBridge5 traded most World Computer-Bridge Championship titles from 2001 to 2015 (Allevy and ICGA pages). BEN (GPL-3.0) uses neural networks for bidding and DDS for play; its README says it cannot use or interpret defensive signals. NooK (NukkAI, April 2022, declarer play only): it played 800 deals against WBridge5 defenders while 8 champions played the same deals; press reports 67 of 80 sets won. I found no primary paper. GIB's extra strength on hard problems came partly from hand-written explanations of opponents' bids.

findings.topic: Double-dummy solver techniques (Bo Haglund's DDS) mapped to dominoes
findings.claim: DDS uses zero-window search with iterative target narrowing, fast quick-trick and later-trick bounds, a TT at trick boundaries with lower and upper bounds, partition search (store only the ranks that mattered, as relative ranks), card equivalence, move ordering, and a per-card double-dummy cost mode for analysis.
sources: Haglund and Hein, Search Algorithms for a Bridge Double Dummy Solver (DDS v2.8 doc, 2014), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dds-bridge/dds/develop/doc/Alg-dds_x.pdf
Haglund and Hein, DDS Performance and Benchmarking, Nov 2014, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dds-bridge/dds/develop/doc/2014-11%20Performance%20and%20Benchmarking.pdf
findings.implication: The solver spec should include: (1) an exact TT key (4 hand masks + canonical ends + mover + passes, plus the boneyard pointer in 1v1) with bound entries; (2) zero-window or MTD search when the objective is a threshold (win/loss or match-equity cutoffs), and a score window otherwise; (3) move ordering (TT move first, then heavier tiles and doubles); (4) cheap bounds, such as immediate domino available or a pip-sum bound; (5) a per-move double-dummy loss for post-game review, shown next to the information-set (single-dummy) loss.
findings.detail: Mapping is my inference. Card equivalence has little analogue in dominoes, because each tile carries two specific numbers. A partition-search analogue (storing which features of the position mattered) is possible but not needed, given millisecond solves. DDS 'play' mode, which scores each played card double-dummy, became 6 to 9 times faster through reuse. Caveat for analysis: double-dummy loss overstates errors made under real uncertainty, so the chess.com-style review must show the information-set evaluation as the primary number.

findings.topic: Symmetry reduction and pip relabeling
findings.claim: Swapping the two ends and rotating seats (with team labels swapped) are exact symmetries. Relabeling the numbers 0-6 keeps the legal-move structure but changes scores (domino pip totals, the tranque pip comparison, and the highest-double opening rule), so it is not a valid search or training symmetry.
sources: Own analysis of the Capi rules in the task spec; TT canonical-end key in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-Adelson-Desktop-personal/8fffa044-f991-4add-a6d7-951296d03a0d/scratchpad/research/algorithms/bench/solve.c
findings.implication: Canonicalize ends (lo, hi) in TT keys and use seat-relative encoding in nets. Use pip relabeling only as a test oracle: complete-line counts per deal must not change under relabeling (with the opener fixed). Never use it to merge TT entries or to augment value training data.
findings.detail: Example: relabeling 6 and 0 swaps which tiles are heavy, so domino scores and tranque winners change, and the first-round opener (highest double) moves. Capicua and pase structure are preserved.

findings.topic: CFR and its search variants (DeepStack, Libratus, Pluribus, ReBeL, Student of Games)
findings.claim: These methods reach equilibrium-quality play in poker. For dominoes they are practical only for late, small subgames or as a research tier: public-belief inputs scale with the number of private hands, and their guarantees cover two-player zero-sum games, so 1v1 is covered but 2v2 teams are not.
sources: Moravcik et al., DeepStack, Science 356:508-513, 2017, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.01724
Brown and Sandholm, Libratus, Science 359:418-424, 2018 (IJCAI 2017 demo https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2017/772)
Brown and Sandholm, Superhuman AI for multiplayer poker (Pluribus), Science 365:885-890, 2019
Brown, Bakhtin, Lerer, Gong, ReBeL, NeurIPS 2020, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.13544
Schmid et al., Student of Games, Science Advances 9(46) eadg3256, 2023, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.03178
findings.implication: Do not plan full-game CFR from the opening. Plan exact game-theoretic solves of small endgames (see the endgame finding), and keep ReBeL/SoG-style 1v1 late-game search as an optional research tier.
findings.detail: DeepStack: 44,852 games vs 33 pros; 492 mbb/g raw, 486 +/- 40 mbb/g with AIVAT; re-solved subgames of about 10^7 decision points in under 5 s on one GTX 1080. Libratus: 120,000 hands, 147 mbb/hand; blueprint plus nested subgame solving plus self-improver. Pluribus: blueprint by MCCFR in 8 days on 64 cores (12,400 CPU core hours, under 512 GB, about $144); 48 mbb/game (SE 25) with AIVAT. ReBeL: 'input ... grows linearly with the number of infostates in a public state'; guarantees only for two-player zero-sum. SoG: beat the PIMC-based Scotland Yard bot PimBot at 55% even when PimBot used 10M simulations. Dominoes sizes (my arithmetic): C(28,7)=1,184,040 possible private hands per player vs 1,326 in heads-up hold'em (893 times more). 2v2 deals: 28!/(7!^4)=4.73e14. One seat's view at the start: 21!/(7!^3)=3.99e8. These sizes collapse quickly as tiles are revealed (df finding). Long et al.'s Skat result shows the practical value: PIMC lost 0.42 tournament points per unresolved deal vs a CFR endgame solution, only 0.063 per deal overall, against a tournament SD of 778 per 180 deals. Fit: (a) 1v1 endgames yes, full game research only; (b) 2v2 see the team-games finding.

findings.topic: 2v2 as an adversarial team game
findings.claim: 2v2 dominoes is zero-sum between teams, but teammates hold private information and coordinate only through public plays. The matching solution concept is the team-maxmin equilibrium with correlation (TMECor), which is hard to compute exactly. Newer representations (team belief DAG) scale with the team's uncommon information.
sources: Celli and Gatti, Computational Results for Extensive-Form Adversarial Team Games, AAAI 2018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06930
Zhang, Farina, Sandholm, Team Belief DAG, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:40996-41018, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/zhang23j.html
Zhang, Carminati et al., Subgame Solving in Adversarial Team Games, NeurIPS 2022, https://www.mit.edu/~gfarina/2022/subgame_solving_teams_neurips22
findings.implication: Do not claim Nash or equilibrium guarantees for 2v2. Offer team-CFR only for small 2v2 endgames as a research tier, and treat the engine controlling both partner seats in self-play as agreeing on a convention in advance.
findings.detail: Celli and Gatti show that losses from limited team communication can grow without bound with tree size. A secondary summary reports FNP-hardness for the correlated case. TB-DAG is a lossless representation that can be exponentially smaller than earlier ones. Partnering humans breaks the 'shared convention' assumption (see the partnership finding).

findings.topic: Exact endgame solving (perfect and imperfect information)
findings.claim: Late in a round, both perfect-information and true imperfect-information solves are cheap enough to compute exactly. That gives ground truth for measuring PIMC error and for post-game analysis.
sources: Own measurements: bench/df.c and bench/stage.c under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-Adelson-Desktop-personal/8fffa044-f991-4add-a6d7-951296d03a0d/scratchpad/research/algorithms/
Long et al., AAAI 2010 (Skat endgame CFR vs PIMC), https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/7562
findings.implication: Step 5 rule: once the number of consistent worlds is at or below a threshold (for example 1e3, typically by a seat's 4th to 5th turn in 2v2), enumerate every world with its inference weight and solve each exactly, removing sampling error. On a held-out endgame set, compute the exact imperfect-information solution (sequence-form LP or CFR for 1v1; team methods for 2v2) and report PIMC's average loss in points/round, using Long et al.'s method.
findings.detail: 2v2 information-set sizes from one seat's view: about 10^3.5 consistent deals at its 4th turn, 10^2.3 at its 5th, 10^1.3 at its 6th (random play, hard constraints only). Bitboards: a 28-bit mask per hand, ends as two 3-bit numbers, all set operations on 32-bit words. Perfect-information solves at 15 tiles left take a median 0.015 ms. Sequence-form LP is the textbook exact method for two-player zero-sum games (Koller, Megiddo, von Stengel 1996); I cite it from memory and did not re-fetch it.

findings.topic: AlphaZero/MuZero-style self-play and imperfect-information limits
findings.claim: AlphaZero and MuZero assume perfect information. Stochastic MuZero adds chance (afterstates) but not hidden information. AlphaZero-like methods for imperfect information are competitive baselines but trail game-theoretic systems.
sources: Antonoglou, Schrittwieser, Ozair, Hubert, Silver, Planning in Stochastic Environments with a Learned Model, ICLR 2022, https://iclr.cc/virtual/2022/poster/6832

Bluml, Czech, Kersting, AlphaZe**: AlphaZero-like baselines for imperfect information games are surprisingly strong, Frontiers in AI 6, 2023, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2023.1014561/pdf
Schmid et al., Student of Games, 2023, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.03178
findings.implication: Use AlphaZero-style learning only inside the PIMC/ISMCTS framework, as a value and policy net over information sets. Do not use it as a standalone perfect-information MCTS over the true state, which would cheat at training time and fuse strategies at play time.
findings.detail: Stochastic MuZero matched or beat the state of the art in 2048 and backgammon and matched MuZero in Go (abstract). AlphaZe** reached win rates against other Stratego bots similar to P2SRO, but lost to P2SRO head to head and was far below DeepNash (abstract). Cost: high (GPU training) for uncertain gain over PIMC. Fit: (a) 1v1 low as a core, medium as a component; (b) 2v2 low as a core, medium as a component.

findings.topic: Deep RL in tile and card games with teams (DouZero, PerfectDou, Suphx)
findings.claim: Self-play deep RL reached top level in DouDizhu, whose two peasants form a team with hidden hands, and in Mahjong, a tile game. The key trick is training with perfect information while acting with imperfect information.
sources: Zha et al., DouZero, ICML 2021, PMLR 139:12333-12344, https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06135
Yang et al., PerfectDou: Dominating DouDizhu with Perfect Information Distillation, NeurIPS 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16406
Li et al., Suphx: Mastering Mahjong with Deep Reinforcement Learning, 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.13590
findings.implication: For step 7, train actor nets that see only their own information set, with a critic that sees all hands (cheap in dominoes, where exact values are available). Use these nets as PIMC/ISMCTS priors, as leaf evaluators, and as the partner and opponent models for policy-based inference.
findings.detail: DouZero: Deep Monte Carlo, one server with 4 GPUs, beat existing DouDizhu AIs within days and ranked 1st of 344 agents on Botzone. PerfectDou: perfect-training, imperfect-execution actor-critic; its paper claims it beats DouZero. Its repo table is ambiguous for one DouZero variant (52.08%), and training code is not released. Suphx: oracle guiding, global reward prediction, run-time policy adaptation; rated above 99.99% of ranked Tenhou players. Cost: high. Fit: (a) 1v1 medium; (b) 2v2 medium to high as the way to learn signaling conventions.

findings.topic: Neural evaluation (NNUE) vs hand-crafted evaluation
findings.claim: NNUE is a CPU-efficient net with an incrementally updated first layer, trained on search evaluations. It gave Stockfish more than 80 Elo. For dominoes, the idea that carries over is training small nets on search outputs; incremental updates matter less.
sources: Chessprogramming wiki, NNUE (Yu Nasu 2018, shogi origin), https://www.chessprogramming.org/NNUE
findings.implication: In 2v2, skip a perfect-information value net, because exact solves are milliseconds. Build small information-set value and policy nets (inputs: 28 tiles x location or known-void features, ends, hand counts, pass history, match score), trained on PIMC and endgame labels. Hand-crafted heuristics serve only as baselines and move ordering.
findings.detail: Stockfish NNUE tests: 92.77 +/- 2.1 Elo (95%) over 60,000 games at 10+0.1 s, 1 thread; 89.47 +/- 2.0 over 40,000 games at 20+0.2 s, 8 threads. The net was trained on evaluations of millions of positions at moderate search depth. NNUE roughly halved search speed yet gained strength (chessprogramming wiki).

findings.topic: Partnership modeling (conventions, Bayesian beliefs, Hanabi-style search)
findings.claim: Cooperative imperfect-information work offers three usable tools: single-agent search against a known partner blueprint with exact Bayesian belief updates (SPARTA), public beliefs conditioned on all agents' actions (BAD), and grounded conventions that work with unfamiliar partners (Off-Belief Learning).
sources: Lerer, Hu, Foerster, Brown, Improving Policies via Search in Cooperative Partially Observable Games (SPARTA), AAAI 2020, https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/6208
Foerster et al., Bayesian Action Decoder for Deep Multi-Agent RL, ICML 2019, PMLR 97:1942-1951
Hu, Lerer, Cui, Pineda, Brown, Foerster, Off-Belief Learning, ICML 2021, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/hu21c.html
findings.implication: In 2v2, keep a belief over hidden hands updated by Bayes with a partner model and an opponent model. Search assuming the partner follows a blueprint that sees only its own information (not an omniscient partner). When the bot partners a human, use a human-play model trained on Capi logs for beliefs. Evaluate with a cross-play matrix (bot+bot, bot+human-model, bot+different-bot).
findings.detail: SPARTA raised Hanabi to 24.61/25 from the previous best 24.08 (abstract). OBL targets zero-shot coordination and avoids arbitrary self-play conventions that break with humans. Skat (Kermit) and Spades (AI Factory) are the closest card-game partnership cases: defender inference gave the largest Skat gain, and partner-visible blunders were the main quality problem in commercial Spades. Domino-specific convention knowledge (for example, playing toward partner's number) is outside this lane and should come from the rules and conventions lane.

findings.topic: Move-generation correctness (perft-style) and differential testing
findings.claim: Chess engines verify move generation with perft: exact counts of leaf nodes at fixed depth, checked against known values, with 'divide' per root move to locate bugs. The dominoes equivalent is per-deal counts of complete play lines and of lines at fixed depth.
sources: Own line counts: bench/solve.c (median 6.32e6 complete play lines per 2v2 deal from the opening; median 2.18e6 distinct states)
findings.implication: Step 0 must ship: (1) perft vectors per seeded deal (lines at depth 1..N and complete lines, with divide output) generated from Capi's packages/engine, which is the spec; (2) differential fuzzing that compares legal-move sets, pass and draw handling, bonuses, and round scores between the new engine and packages/engine at every step of 1e6 or more random rounds per mode, with 0 mismatches allowed; (3) invariant tests (end swap, seat rotation, line counts unchanged by pip relabeling); (4) solver vs naive minimax on small positions.
findings.detail: Hashing perft gives about 1.5 to 4 times speedup with a small chance of wrong counts (wiki). Use it only after the unhashed counts match. Capi code is the spec for rules, not evidence of Dominican rules.

findings.topic: Strength testing: SPRT (fishtest), Elo, confidence intervals
findings.claim: Stockfish accepts changes by sequential probability ratio tests on color-reversed game pairs (pentanomial model) at short and long time controls, with gainer and non-regression bounds in Elo.
sources: Fishtest wiki, Creating my first test (STC 10+0.1, LTC 60+0.6; non-regression example <-1.75, 0.25>), https://github.com/official-stockfish/fishtest/wiki/Creating-my-first-test
Chessprogramming wiki, SPRT (gainer/non-regression bound pairs, alpha=beta=0.05), https://www.chessprogramming.org/Sequential_Probability_Ratio_Test
findings.implication: The match harness should treat one duplicate pair (the same deal with teams swapped, or 1v1 hands swapped with the same boneyard order) as the unit, like fishtest's game pair. Run SPRT on the per-pair point margin or on the match-win result, with stated H0/H1 bounds and alpha=beta=0.05. Report mean points/round and match-win rate with 95% CIs, and convert win rate to Elo only alongside the CI.
findings.detail: Example bound pairs on the wiki: gainer [0, 2] or [0.5, 2.5] with non-regression [-1.75, 0.25]. Units for dominoes should be points/round and match-win probability, not chess Elo; convert to Elo only to compare bots.

findings.topic: Variance reduction for random deals (duplicate, AIVAT, control variates), with own measurement
findings.claim: Duplicate formats and AIVAT are the standard ways to cut luck. In my dominoes tests duplicate replay helped only modestly (1.1 to 1.65 times fewer games) and simple deal features explained about 5% of variance, so the engine's own value estimates must drive the control variates.
sources: Burch, Schmid, Moravcik, Bowling, AIVAT, AAAI-17 workshop / AAAI 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06915
Moravcik et al. 2017 (AIVAT 85% SD reduction, significance with 3,000 games), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.01724
ACPC duplicate matches, e.g. Zinkevich competition paper, https://www.martin.zinkevich.org/publications/competition.pdf
Own: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-Adelson-Desktop-personal/8fffa044-f991-4add-a6d7-951296d03a0d/scratchpad/research/algorithms/bench/dup.c (400,000 deals per pairing) and pimc.c results
findings.implication: Plan sample sizes of thousands of rounds per comparison. Resolving a 1 point/round edge at 2 SE with SD 28 points/round needs about (2x28/1)^2 = 3,136 rounds; at 0.5 points/round, about 12,500. Implement AIVAT-style correction using the engine's own value of the deal and of 1v1 draws (chance events) and of its own stochastic choices, and keep duplicate seating for fairness.
findings.detail: Own, simplified 2v2 rules: SD of one round's margin 27.4 to 32.2 points; SD of a duplicate pair mean 15.3 to 21.9; games-needed ratio (independent / duplicate) 1.08 for heaviest vs random, 1.11 for heavy+doubles vs heaviest, 1.65 for identical bots. Linear control variate on opener team, pip difference, and doubles difference: ratio 1.05 to 1.06; the opener team gains about 6 to 7 points/round. With PIMC20 in the match: SD 37.8 per round and 24.4 per pair (ratio about 1.2). Heuristic edges are small: heaviest-tile vs random +1.39 points/round; heavy+doubles vs heaviest +2.40. AIVAT is provably unbiased and needed more than 10 times fewer hands in no-limit poker (abstract).

findings.topic: Match-level objective and win probability
findings.claim: With targets of 100 or 200 and bonuses that cannot win a game, a round's value to a player depends on the match score, so the engine should maximize match-win probability via a match equity table rather than raw round points. Backgammon engines do exactly this.
sources: GNU Backgammon manual, Match Winning Chance, https://www.gnu.org/software/gnubg/manual/html_node/Match-Winning-Chance.html
Rockwell-Kazaross match equity table (rollouts of about 39,000 games per score in a 15-point match, extrapolated to 25), https://bkgm.com/articles/Kazaross/RockwellKazarossMET/index.html
findings.implication: Have the engine compute a dominoes match equity table W(my score, their score, target, who leads next) by simulation or DP over the engine's own round-score distribution, applying the 'bonus not paid at target' rule. Use W of the terminal round outcome as the leaf utility in late-match positions. Report win probability calibrated by Brier score and reliability curves on held-out games.
findings.detail: Mapping to dominoes is my inference. Near the target, maximizing expected points and maximizing match-win probability can choose different moves; for example, a capicua bonus that would reach the target is worth 0.

findings.topic: How to prove 'beats elite humans' with few human games
findings.claim: NooK's 2022 evaluation had champions and the AI play the same deals against the same fixed bot opponents, and compared results, with no head-to-head games needed. This is a paired design that cuts variance with limited human time.
sources: LessWrong critique of the NooK result, https://lesswrong.com/posts/yHxmJch8dJoH6dwwz
findings.implication: For the human benchmark, run duplicate sessions where an elite human pair and the engine pair each play the same seeded deals against the same fixed bot opponents. Compare per-deal margins (paired test with AIVAT-style correction) and keep Capi rated play as a second signal.
findings.detail: NooK played 800 deals and each champion played 100; press reports 67 of 80 sets won. Critics note a simplified setting (declarer play only, no head-to-head), so state the scope of any claim.

findings.topic: 1v1 specifics: the boneyard as chance and hidden information
findings.claim: In 1v1, drawing is forced and the drawn tiles are seen only by the drawer, so draws are chance events that are only partly observable. Full determinization (opponent hand plus draw order) lets each sampled world foresee future draws, and the exact solve has a heavy tail.
sources: Cowling et al. 2012 (partially observable moves, MO-ISMCTS), https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75048/
Own: bench/solve.c 1v1 results (median 0.46 ms, max 1.09 s per determinized deal)
findings.implication: In 1v1, sample opponent hand and draw order jointly but consistent with the history: every draw event proves the drawer held no tile matching the ends at that time, and the shared stack interleaves both players' draws. Cap solver nodes. Compare against ISMCTS with partially observable draw moves, and against expectimax chance nodes over draws in the subsolve, by SPRT.
findings.detail: Hand sizes can grow toward 21 tiles through draws, which raises branching and causes the solve tail. The unknown pool shrinks slowly while the boneyard lasts, so df is lower than in 2v2 and PIMC is expected to be relatively weaker. The expectation is my inference and was not measured.

findings.topic: Domino-specific algorithmic prior art
findings.claim: Published algorithmic work on dominoes is thin and old. I found no published PIMC, ISMCTS, or CFR engine for Dominican dominoes with measured expert strength.
sources: A learning program which plays partnership dominoes, Communications of the ACM 16(8), 1973, https://cacmb4.acm.org/magazines/1973/8/11845-a-learning-program-which-plays-partnership-dominoes/abstract
Myers, Outperforming Game Theoretic Play with Opponent Modeling in Two Player Dominoes, AFIT MS thesis, 2014, https://scholar.afit.edu/etd/617
IEEE paper comparing four agents for two-player Brazilian dominoes over 1,000,000 matches (abstract via Infona), https://www.infona.pl/resource/bwmeta1.element.ieee-art-000006855868
findings.implication: The engine's novelty claim (SDE2 portfolio) can rest on bringing modern imperfect-information search, inference, and evaluation methods to Dominican dominoes. The prompt should still have the build session check the domino-prior-art lane's results.
findings.detail: The 1973 program used a strategy signature table with adaptive weights and won about two-thirds of its tournament games (abstract). The AFIT thesis found opponent modeling gained score over a Nash player in two-player dominoes. My searches surfaced only small GitHub projects using ISMCTS or expectiminimax. Absence of results in my searches is not proof that none exist.

open_questions: Are the own benchmark numbers confirmed under exact Capi rules (later rounds led by the previous winner, how bonuses interact with the round winner, the target rule, 1v1 opening and draw details)? My code is a simplified reimplementation; the build session should regenerate them against packages/engine.
How large is the PIMC-to-exact-solution gap in 2v2 and 1v1 endgames (Long et al.'s Skat-style measurement)? It was not measured.
What is the 1v1 disambiguation factor, and how much does PIMC lose from foreseeing future draws? Neither was measured; a history-consistent 1v1 world sampler was not built.
Does a PIMC100 self-play null test (expected mean 0 points/round) pass? It was started as a harness sanity check and stopped before finishing.
Which partner signaling conventions do elite Dominican players use, and how should a bot interpret a human partner's plays? This needs the conventions lane and Capi game logs.
What compute budget per move is acceptable on device vs server? This sets worlds per move and decides whether learned nets are needed for latency (runtime-fit lane).
Primary sources were read only at the abstract or secondary level for NooK (press only), the BAD/OBL details, TMECor complexity (secondary summary), and the Rockwell-Kazaross table method.

lanes.summary: The upstream check is clear. No strong dominoes engine exists for Dominican rules or for any Latin partnership variant. No source reports a domino AI tested against elite humans with measured results. The only claim of beating champions is Smith's 1973 BASIC program (CACM 16(8)), which won about two-thirds of its tournament games. The strongest measured open-source work on Latin double-six partnership play is fabianruiz3/puerto-rican-dominoes (MIT, Aug 2026). Its 24-world PIMC bot wins 87.9% of matches against a greedy heuristic (95% CI 85.2-90.1%, 700 matches), and it beats an MCCFR bot 76.5% head to head. Its bot uses Puerto Rican scoring and was never tested against humans or other engines. abw333/dominoes (PyPI dominoes 6.1.0, last commit 2018) runs PIMC with alpha-beta and reports no strength. Its scoring is close to Capi's, but it has no bonuses and resolves a tranque by team totals. OpenSpiel team_dominoes (Apache-2.0, 2024) settles every terminal by comparing team pips, which conflicts with Capi's rules. The commercial apps (RDomino, DR Dominoes, Capicúa: Dominó Dominicano, JuegoDomino.com, Don Naipe, Flyclops) advertise smart bots, coaches or AI game review, and none publishes a method or a measured strength.
