Verdict: the "strongest Dominican dominoes engine" slot is open, and the public bar is "beats a greedy heuristic" (high confidence for the open web; private engines cannot be ruled out). Prior art does fix the method: exact determinization samplers with a never-peeks test, mirrored deals with seat swaps and CIs, a perfect-information oracle as the ceiling, calibration checks, and a match-equity table (SBEngine, All Fives). The fabianruiz3 results warn against coarse CFR abstractions. For Job 2, the richest strategy sources are Venezuelan (dominoarteociencia summarizing Simosa Alarcón, Zaibert, Balestrini, Delgado and Lugo), Cuban (EFDeportes 2012, UCI 2022) and Dominican (Acento 2025: cabeza/encabezado, mano, manito, frente, trancar). They give exact pass-inference combinatorics, opening-lead rules, double-hanging risk, seat roles and tranque criteria. Parra & Trucco (arXiv 2025) supply full published deals: the 1965 "partida inmortal" and two minimal-tranque deals. They also prove an invariant: a tranque always has equal ends with all 7 tiles of that number on the board. Together these give hard rules and inference fixtures. Expert opening rules work only as soft agreement tests, because the authors disagree. No collection of puzzle positions or tournament move records was found.

findings.topic: Job1 verdict: is the strongest-Dominican-engine slot open
findings.claim: Yes. No public engine implements Dominican rules (capicúa, pase corrido, pase de salida, blocker-vs-next-player tranque) with search and measured strength, and no source reports any domino AI matched against elite humans with numbers.
sources: GitHub repo search, PyPI simple index, npm and crates.io registry searches, arXiv API, OpenAlex API (all run 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: The prompt should say the engine is built from scratch, with Capi's packages/engine as the only rules oracle. It should state the public bar honestly: the best published Latin partnership bot only beats a greedy heuristic. 'Beats elite humans' must then be shown with Capi's own human games, because no external benchmark engine exists.
findings.detail: Search coverage: GitHub (name, description and README searches in English and Spanish), PyPI (142 domino-named packages scanned; only 'dominoes' and 'all-fives-domino' are games), npm (domino-ai, domino-bot, doble9 are minor), crates.io (none relevant), arXiv (only 2502.06790 and 1011.0187 are tile-game papers), OpenAlex (about 15 dominoes-AI papers, listed in other findings), plus app-store listings. Several small hobby repos appeared in 2026 (ondrej-gvozdjak/dominoes-engine created 2026-10-22, pauklo10/ficha 2026-02-10, MarAlons0/domino-advisor pushed today). The niche is getting attention but is not yet taken. Caveat: closed engines inside commercial apps cannot be inspected.

findings.topic: Strongest measured open-source Latin partnership bot (benchmark target)
findings.claim: fabianruiz3/puerto-rican-dominoes: a PIMC bot (24 sampled worlds, each solved exactly with best response vs a heuristic model) wins 87.9% of matches vs greedy; MCCFR bot 60.7%; PIMC beats CFR 76.5% head to head; a perfect-information oracle wins 300/300 vs greedy.
findings.implication: Use it as a design reference and an optional cross-check, not a dependency, because its rules are Puerto Rican, not Capi's. Copy its evaluation method: pooled seeds, seat-swapped pairs, 95% CIs, an oracle ceiling, and a never-peeks test that rearranges the hidden tiles behind an identical public record and asserts the move does not change.
findings.detail: Numbers: match win rate vs greedy, pooled over seeds, each pairing played twice with seats swapped. PIMC at 24 worlds: 87.9% [85.2, 90.1], 700 matches, about 7 ms per move (hardware not stated). At 12 worlds 84.6% [81.7, 87.1]; at 6 worlds 79.5% [75.3, 83.2]. CFR: 60.7% [58.6, 62.6] over 2,300 matches. Its policy is 20 MB (688k info sets) from 4.8M traversals (32 cores, 1 hour). Rules, from scoring.py: a winning team scores only the losers' pips, on a domino and on a tranque. Capicú counts when the ends are equal after the play. Chuchazo bonus for the double blank. Modeling: the partner and opponents are assumed to play the heuristic. Author's stated weakness: no information-gathering plays.

findings.topic: CFR abstraction pathology in partnership dominoes
findings.claim: In the fabianruiz3 experiments, a coarse CFR abstraction trained longer gets worse. The 'tiny' level falls from 56.3% to 42.5% vs greedy as traversals grow from 384k to 4.8M. Coverage ranks the abstractions in exactly the wrong order.
sources: https://github.com/fabianruiz3/puerto-rican-dominoes (README sections 'The abstraction is not a coverage problem', 'Training a lossy abstraction longer makes it worse')
findings.implication: The prompt should not make abstracted tabular CFR the main engine. Prefer search on the real position (PIMC or ISMCTS, later with learned evaluation). If CFR-style training is used, judge each policy only by playing it in arena matches, never by its convergence or coverage.
findings.detail: Results at equal compute (4.8M traversals): tiny 82,644 info sets, 100% decisions answered, 42.5% vs greedy. Compact 4.28M info sets, 48.8%. Coarse 13.75M info sets, 59.4%. The author also notes that CFR's guarantees do not cover a 2v2 team game. Single source, not peer reviewed, hence medium confidence.

findings.topic: Python 'dominoes' library (abw333, author Alan Wagner)
findings.claim: PyPI dominoes 6.1.0 (MIT) models 4-player double-six partnership play 'commonly played in San Juan, Puerto Rico'. Its search players are 'omniscient' (alpha-beta with all hands visible) and 'probabilistic_alphabeta' (samples consistent hands and votes for the move most often optimal). It reports no strength.
sources: abw333 dominoes/players.py and dominoes/search.py and dominoes/game.py (read 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: Its scoring is the closest public match to Capi's, but it lacks bonuses, the first-round rules and the blocker-vs-next-player tranque, so it cannot serve as an oracle. Use it only as a low baseline, voting-PIMC versus value-averaging PIMC. Note that deepcopy-based search in Python is too slow to set any performance bar.
findings.detail: Scoring in game.py: the player who goes out scores the sum of all remaining hands, partner included (line 342), as in Capi. A stuck game compares team totals (players 0+2 vs 1+3); the lower total wins all pips and a tie scores 0. That differs from Capi (blocker vs next player, tie to la mano). Its probabilistic_alphabeta respects hand sizes and passes, enumerates all possible hands by default, and returns the voting winner, not the expected value.

findings.topic: OpenSpiel team_dominoes / block_dominoes
findings.claim: OpenSpiel (Apache-2.0) includes python team_dominoes (4 players, double-six, all tiles dealt) and block_dominoes, added by Brunozml in PR #1211 (merged 2024-05-31). Its returns() settles every terminal, domino or block, by comparing team pip totals, so a player who goes out can still lose.
findings.implication: Do not reuse OpenSpiel's rules. One optional, resume-worthy extension is a faithful 'capi_dominoes' OpenSpiel game wrapping Capi's rules, which gives free access to OpenSpiel's ISMCTS, CFR and NFSP baselines. It must be checked against packages/engine.
findings.detail: The code checks only whether a player emptied his hand or the game is stuck. It then compares the team pip sums: the lower team gets the other team's sum, and a tie gives 0. No bonuses, no first-lead rule.

findings.topic: Other open-source dominoes AIs (none strong, all small)
findings.claim: Every other public dominoes AI found is a hobby or course project. None has a license-clean, rules-compatible, measured-strong engine for Dominican play.
sources: https://github.com/angeris/DominAI (Stanford CS221 2016, Angeris & Li, no license) and https://angeris.github.io/papers/dominai_poster.pdf
https://github.com/imadtg/domino-ai (2-player draw minimax in C, MIT, 2026-09-22; npm domino-ai WASM)
https://github.com/atelognomist/Dominant (Rust ISMCTS spec only, no code, 2026-07-16)
https://github.com/matcom/domino (Univ. of Havana course spec 2022, MIT)
findings.implication: No code reuse is recommended. Several repos have no license (7 Fichas, DominAI, SRogDev, isaacbuckman) or use AGPL (benabraham-ai), which rules out copying. Treat them only as reading and competitor context.
findings.detail: Reported numbers: 7 Fichas Master (ISMCTS at 1,000 iterations, reward 0.8*win + 0.2*margin) beat its earlier priority hybrid 58.8% (CI 54.5-63.1) over 500 matches. 1,000 vs 5,000 iterations scored 65.6% vs 63.4% (500 matches, indistinguishable). 10,000 iterations regressed from garbage-collection pauses, with worst-case latency about 25 s per decision (browser JS). DominAI PIMC team vs greedy team: 73-26-1 over 100 games (100 samples). SRogDev 1v1 MAPPO: 60.2% vs random and 48.2% vs greedy (double-9). The Dominican game repos (2mino, grullon68-arch, Phamton140, JulioMarquezH) only have heuristic bots.

findings.topic: Stockfish-style dominoes engine design precedent (different variant)
findings.claim: Mawxy/SBEngine is a C++20 'Stockfish-style' engine for 2-player All Fives (Spectacular Bid). It runs PIMC over constraint-consistent deals, with negamax alpha-beta, iterative deepening, a transposition table, NNUE horizon evaluation, an info-set value network and a match equity table that gives P(win game). It also has a UCI-like JSON CLI, a WASM browser build and a replay mode that grades each decision.
findings.implication: This is the closest architectural template for the Capi engine. Borrow these pieces: a text protocol like UCI, PIMC plus alpha-beta first, a match equity table for targets 100 and 200 so every move shows P(win game), a calibration check of the reported probabilities, a game-review grade (inaccuracy, mistake, blunder), and generation gating where a new model must beat the current best head to head. Do not copy its code: it has no license and bundles third-party code.
findings.detail: Reported: search matches brute-force minimax on 300 random small positions. +2.05 chips per hand (se 0.19) vs greedy over 300 mirrored deal pairs. Zero inference errors in 5,800 decisions. Calibration over 300 self-play games (about 8,500 positions): predicted 7% happened 13%, predicted 91% happened 86%. Vs HaviEngine: 19-1 over 20 games (old version with a sign bug) and 16-4 with the bug fixed. NNUE training round 1 (36 h) gave about +0.10 chips per hand in generation 1, then plateaued. The author lists strategy fusion as a known limitation.

findings.topic: Academic dominoes AI literature (thin, mostly variant-specific)
findings.claim: Peer-reviewed dominoes AI is sparse and weak. The relevant items are Smith 1973 (partnership, signature tables), Antonio et al. 2011 IEEE CIG (GA-tuned evaluation, 4-sided Amazonas partnership), Silva 2015 UFAM thesis (expectiminimax, 4-sided), da Cruz et al. 2013 (2-player, Minas Gerais), Myers 2014 AFIT thesis (2-player, opponent modeling vs a Nash player), Moreno-Montiel et al. 2020 Computación y Sistemas (Monte Carlo strategy comparison), the UCI Cuba 2022 thesis (MCTS 1v1 in Unity) and Medina et al. 2024 (NAO robot). None tests Latin partnership double-six against strong humans with modern search.
findings.implication: A rigorous engine with documented methods and honest CIs would itself be a publishable contribution (for example an IEEE CoG short paper or an arXiv preprint). The prompt can ask for a reproducible eval report as a deliverable.
findings.detail: Numbers with basis. Smith 1973: wins 'approximately two-thirds' of tournament games and 'has defeated championship players' (from the abstract; full text blocked by ACM 403). Antonio 2011: GA-tuned team won more than 70% of 5,000 matches. Silva 2015: best strategy won 72.04% of 5,000 matches vs the basic strategy and 58.34% vs the GA strategy. da Cruz 2013: 1,000,000 matches per pairing; Boltzmann roulette strategy best. Moreno-Montiel 2020 (Mexican rules, 4 individual players): 'Tirar la ficha más acompañada' best at 31-34% win probability, runs of 5,000 to 40,000 games; the opening strategy made no difference. UCI 2022: depth 8 means 38,358 simulations in 7.88 s, with no win rates reported. Medina 2024: decision-making error 3.37%.

findings.topic: Complexity result
findings.claim: Demaine, Ma, Waingarten (FUN 2014) prove that perfect-information dominoes is in P for one player, NP-complete for cooperative multiplayer play, and PSPACE-complete for competitive multiplayer play, and the results extend to team play.
findings.implication: This supports the resume framing and justifies search plus heuristics over closed-form solving. Small practical double-six endgames stay exactly solvable, since a perfect-information hand is about 22 plies with branching about 2.5 in the fabianruiz3 measurements.
findings.detail: The hardness concerns generalized tile sets. The double-six game tree is small per determinization, which is why PIMC with exact solving works.

findings.topic: Commercial apps and analysis tools (competitors, unmeasured)
findings.claim: Dominican and Latin apps advertise strong or smart bots and coaching, but none publishes an algorithm or a measured strength. Two offer analysis features that compete with the planned post-game tool: JuegoDomino.com (AI move-by-move game review, 'expert robot' hints, expert-annotated 'Mesas Didácticas', subscription) and Capicúa: Dominó Dominicano ('Don Capicúa' coach for hand replays).
sources: https://apps.apple.com/do/app/dr-dominoes/id6803592246 (v2.7.1, Oct 14; 111 ratings, 4.2 average; claims its AI counts tiles and tracks plays)
https://apps.apple.com/app/id523001403 (Flyclops Domino!, 5 levels Easy to Beast)
findings.implication: The product pitch should stand on measurable claims the competitors lack: published win rates with CIs vs baselines, calibrated win probability on every move, and transparent game review. Listing claims are marketing and should never be used as strength benchmarks.
findings.detail: Download counts from the search snippet: Flyclops 5M+ on Google Play, Maysalward Dominoes 10M+. Not verified per listing, and neither app plays Dominican rules. The Google Play pages could not be read by WebFetch (truncated), so the Don Naipe details come from the listing summary and the donnaipe.com blog. Dates on the App Store pages show month and day only.

findings.topic: 1v1 (draw game) prior art
findings.claim: For 2-player draw dominoes the prior art is thinner still: imadtg/domino-ai (C minimax, MIT), satpro131 (ISMC with 800 rollouts per move), Ludii's 2-player Block, the UCI 2022 thesis (MCTS), Myers 2014 (opponent modeling) and SBEngine (All Fives with boneyard). None uses Capi's rule that the draw stops at the first playable tile, combined with Capi's bonuses.
findings.implication: The prompt should require draw-aware inference for 1v1. A draw proves the drawer held no tile matching either end at that moment. Every tile drawn before the playable one also failed to match, and that tile is then forced into play. SBEngine states the same constraint for All Fives: drawing or passing proves the opponent held nothing matching the open ends.
findings.detail: Inference about Capi 1v1: because the draw stops at the first playable tile and the player must play, the k-1 drawn tiles and the whole earlier hand lack both end numbers. The determinization sampler must enforce this as a hard constraint on the opponent's hidden hand.

findings.topic: Rule invariant for tests: tranque geometry (published proof)
findings.claim: Parra & Trucco (arXiv 2502.06790, 2025) prove that a blocked hand always ends with both board ends showing the same number k, with all 7 tiles containing k on the board. A tranque needs at least 10 tiles on the board, and the board pips sum to at least 6k+42, so the minimum is 42.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.06790 (Parra & Trucco, Universidad Austral de Chile, 2025), Prop. 2.1 and 2.2
findings.implication: Add property-based tests: whenever packages/engine or the search engine declares a tranque, assert equal ends, all 7 k-tiles on the board, board tile count ≥ 10 and board pips ≥ 6k+42. In Capi, where the tranque winner takes all pips in all hands, the base tranque payout is then at most 168-42 = 126 pips (inference), plus any bonuses.
findings.detail: Parity argument: each number appears 8 times across the 28 tiles. The proof does not depend on the number of players or a boneyard, provided a tranque means no unplayed tile fits either end, as in Capi's definition (inference). EFDeportes (Cuba 2012) independently cites '126 points' as the maximum closing, which matches 168-42 under all-pips scoring.

findings.topic: Published full deals usable as rule-oracle fixtures
findings.claim: Parra & Trucco reproduce three complete 2v2 deals with all four hands and the full play and pass sequence: the 1965 'partida inmortal' (from Miguel Delgado, 'Dominó sin barreras', 2006) and two minimal-tranque deals. These are the only published complete game records found.
findings.implication: Encode these deals as replay fixtures (seats P1..P4, P1+P3 a team, P1 leads in a non-first round, play order P1, P2, P3, P4). Expected scores under Capi rules must come from running packages/engine. My hand-derived values below are for cross-checking only and must not be trusted as ground truth.
findings.detail: Immortal game. Hands: P1 [1-1,4-0,3-1,0-5,0-0,0-2,0-6]; P2 [5-5,6-5,5-4,5-3,6-3,4-3,3-3]; P3 [1-0,0-3,5-1,2-5,2-3,2-2,1-2]; P4 [1-4,2-4,4-4,4-6,2-6,1-6,6-6]. Order: P1 1-1, P2 pass, P3 1-0, P4 1-4; P1 4-0, P2 pass, P3 0-3, P4 pass; P1 3-1, P2 pass, P3 5-1, P4 pass; P1 0-5, P2/P3/P4 pass; P1 0-0, P2/P3/P4 pass; P1 0-2, P2 pass, P3 2-5, P4 pass; P1 0-6 goes out. Paper: 111 points (P2+P4 pips). My Capi-rule derivation (inference): pase de salida +25, two pases corridos +50, domino = all remaining pips 60+12+51 = 123, last tile not capicúa (ends 5 and 0 before it). Minimal tranque A: P1 [0-0,0-3,5-6,6-6,5-5,4-4,3-3], P2 [0-1,3-4,6-0,2-2,1-1,4-1,6-4], P3 [1-2,4-0,6-3,5-4,6-2,3-2,5-3], P4 [2-0,0-5,6-1,2-5,5-1,3-1,4-2]. Play: 0-0, 0-1, 1-2, 2-0, 0-3, 3-4, 4-0, 0-5, 5-6, 6-0, locked by P2. Derived Capi result: P2 has 21 pips vs P3 39, so team P2/P4 takes 126. The 107 deal (P1 0-0 ... P1 0-2 locks; blocker P1 has 5 pips vs P2 50) derives to 126 + pase de salida 25 for team P1/P3. The paper's own scoring gives 107.

findings.topic: Pass-inference combinatorics (exact, testable)
findings.claim: Venezuelan-school deduction rules state that a pass proves the player holds no tile with either open number. Passing on 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 numbers leaves 21, 15, 10, 6 or 3 candidate tiles. If three players pass on the same number, the fourth holds every remaining tile of it.
findings.implication: Build these in as unit tests for the belief and constraint module. The counts follow from (7-s)(8-s)/2 tiles avoiding s numbers. Also add the page's worked example as a sampler test: 4-1, 4-3 and 4-5 played, you hold 4-4 and 4-2, partner passed on 4s, right-hand opponent passed on 6s. Then 4-6 must be with the left-hand opponent.
findings.detail: The same page lists probabilistic deductions, useful as soft priors in the sampler. An opener who leads a double probably holds 1 to 3 more of that number. A mixed-tile lead implies at least one more tile of each half. A later double played on one of the opener's numbers suggests a singleton. Skipping a natural play is a 'hidden pass'. A player who blocks an opponent's suit may be shedding a void rather than showing strength.

findings.topic: Expert concept: la salida (opening lead) and reading the partner's first play
findings.claim: Venezuelan authors (Simosa Alarcón 'El Tigre de Carayaca', Zaibert, Balestrini, Delgado, Fernández Porras, Lugo), as summarized by dominoarteociencia, generally lead the highest accompanied double. With no usable double they lead the mixed tile best supported in both halves. They disagree on leading a lone double. Named special leads exist: 'salida mata doble' and 'salida Almodóvar' (linked to Puerto Rico). There are rules for a 'violín' (5 or more of one number). Pagat and Cuban and Mexican sources agree on leading strength, 'la ficha más acompañada'.
sources: https://repositorio.uci.cu/bitstream/123456789/10605/1/6-TD_9864_22.pdf (UCI 2022, 'salir con la ficha más acompañada', 'la que estorba')
findings.implication: Feature: lead quality, meaning the hand's support count for each half of the led tile and the double's support. Test: a soft 'book agreement' suite of lead positions (two doubles with unequal support: lead the better supported one; six of a number without its double: lead the off-number tile; seven of a number: lead its double). Report the agreement rate, never pass or fail, because the experts disagree. In Capi only later rounds allow a free lead (round 1 auto-places the highest double).
findings.detail: Responses by seat (28 tips #16): la mano plays for himself, the second seat punishes la mano, la mano's partner supports him, and the postre (fourth seat) tries to make la mano pass. Zaibert: answer an opponent's lead from a higher number, and the partner's lead from a lower one.

findings.topic: Expert concept: doubles, ahorcar (hanging) and protecting them
findings.claim: A double is 'ahorcado' (hanged) when all six other tiles of its number are on the board. Risk to your own double is low when it is alone, peaks with 3 accompanying tiles, and is near zero with 4 or more. Chase an opponent's double only when you know where it is and are sure you can close the number, mainly 6-6 and 5-5 (sometimes 4-4 and 3-3). Cuban coaching names the matching skills 'correr el doble' and 'proteger el doble del salidor'.
sources: https://www.efdeportes.com/efd168/la-tactica-del-juego-de-domino.htm (Durruthy Rodríguez et al., EFDeportes 168, May 2012, Cuba)
findings.implication: Feature: for each double in hand, a stranded-double risk built from unseen tiles of its number not in my hand, how many ends show it, and my support count. Feature: a hanging opportunity, meaning I can close a number while a known or likely opponent holds its double. Test positions: (a) the engine can hang a known opponent 6-6 by playing the last free tile of 6s, (b) the engine must shed a 'ficha falla' (EFDeportes example: when an opponent runs the 5-5 and you hold two 5s, play the 5-1 at once). In Capi a hanged opponent double also stays in the pot the winner collects (inference).
findings.detail: The risk curve (peak at 3 accompanying tiles) is expert opinion and should be checked on engine self-play statistics, not hard-coded.

findings.topic: Expert concept: cabeza / encabezado / dekabes (Dominican) and firme
findings.claim: Dominican usage (Roberto Guzmán, Acento, 2025-03-02): a 'cabeza' is a board end with only one tile of that number left, and the player who made it while keeping that last tile is 'encabezado'. 'Dekabes' (a Haitian domino term) means winning two ways at once, that is, two heads. Cuban coaching calls holding back a tile for the partner 'firme'. The 7 Fichas repo defines 'firme' as holding all remaining tiles of a number on an open end.
findings.implication: Feature: the count of open ends where I hold the last unseen tile of that number ('heads'), and whether my partner probably does. Test: endgames where creating two heads forces a domino and the engine must find it from counting alone, with the opponents' hands hidden. These are good tests of the counting and belief code, not only of search.
findings.detail: Exact Acento wording: a tile on the table 'a la que solo corresponde una de la misma pinta' is 'cabeza'. The player 'se guardó la última ficha de esa pinta' and 'está encabezado'.

findings.topic: Expert concept: counting (conteo) and fallo (void)
findings.claim: Counting is central in all schools. Cuban drills count pips on the board to deduce the unplayed total (168 in total: 100 played leaves 68). Venezuelan tips warn against voids ('falla' or 'fallo') early, especially for la mano. Against an opponent's number, play the tile that leaves you void in it, so you never have to open it. Avoid the 'minga' (a tile whose two numbers you hold only once each) early.
sources: https://sites.google.com/site/dominoarteociencia/anuncio/lasalida (glossary: falla/fallo = a suit with no tiles)
findings.implication: Features: remaining count per number (unseen and not in my hand), known voids per seat, own void count, minga count. Tests: the belief module must report exact remaining pip totals and per-number counts in every position. A replay of the published deals must match a hand count.
findings.detail: The 28 tips have no named author. Tip 11 (risk depends on the score) supports a match-equity objective.

findings.topic: Expert concept: forcing passes and cuadrar
findings.claim: Sources name forcing passes as an expert skill: 'pasar al oponente' (UCI 2022), the postre trying to make la mano pass, and 'cuadrar', which makes both ends the same number or numbers the next opponent lacks (7 Fichas). 'Cuadres' (Venezuelan tips) help the partner play an awkward double, force the opponents to pass, win a firme or force out a key tile.
findings.implication: In Capi, forcing passes scores directly: pase corrido is +25 when the other three pass, and pase de salida is +25. Features: P(next seat passes) and P(all three others pass) from the belief state, given a move. Tests: positions where known voids make a move force a pase corrido (+25) and the engine must prefer it at equal hand value. Apply the rule that a bonus reaching the target is not paid.
findings.detail: Inference: because Capi's pase corrido can repeat, a seat that can make the board unplayable for all three others gains repeated +25 swings. Search must model bonus accrual exactly, together with the cap that bonuses never win the game.

findings.topic: Expert concept: when to go for a tranque
findings.claim: Sources advise closing ('cerrar' or 'trancar') with a light hand once 4 or 5 tiles of a number are out (UCI 2022). Compare your likely remaining pips with the next opponent's before blocking (FichaFlow, a Dominican app site, 2025-26). Dominicans 'trancar' on purpose to count the tantos (Acento 2025). An early block ('tranco temprano') is a recognized move (El Inmobiliario 2026).
findings.implication: Feature: whether a locking tile is available, my pips vs the distribution of the next player's pips from the beliefs, and whether my side is la mano (Capi gives equal pips to la mano). Tests: (a) locking with known-lower pips must be chosen, (b) locking with likely-higher pips must be avoided, (c) equal-pips positions differ by whether the blocker's side is la mano. Going out on the locking tile counts as a domino in Capi and needs its own test.
findings.detail: FichaFlow is an app-marketing site with mostly unsourced claims, so give it low weight. Its tranque tie rule ('house rule: tie to the blocker') differs from Capi's (tie to la mano), and Capi's rule governs.

findings.topic: Expert concept: playing to the partner, repite / mata, seat roles, signals
findings.claim: The sources agree. Repeat the partner's lead number unless he signals a weak lead. Punish ('castigar' or 'mata') the opponents' numbers. Do not reopen a number your partner passed on. Block the right-hand opponent's number before the left-hand one ('dejar correr los palos'). With a weak hand, give the initiative to the partner. Signal what you hold through your tile choices. Covert 'señas' between partners count as cheating.
findings.implication: Features: team ownership of each number (who introduced or repeated it), partner's known voids, and whether a move reopens a number the partner passed on. These suit move explanations in the analysis UI. Strength should come from search over beliefs, and conventions should enter as sampler priors, not hard rules. Pensada (timing tells) is out of scope for the engine.
findings.detail: The ISMCTS of 7 Fichas weights its sampler by suit affinity: 2.0x for a double lead, 1.5x for a mixed lead, 1.2x for introducing a number. That project offers a starting prior to tune, not evidence.

findings.topic: Named heuristics usable as baseline bots
findings.claim: Two named heuristics recur in sources and code: 'bota gorda' (dump the highest-pip tile) and 'tirar la ficha más acompañada' (play the tile best supported in your hand). Moreno-Montiel 2020 found 'más acompañada' the best of its tested strategies.
findings.implication: The baseline ladder in the prompt: random, bota gorda, más acompañada, a rule bot built from the concepts above, voting PIMC (abw333 style), value-averaging PIMC, ISMCTS, then the final engine. Add a perfect-information oracle as the ceiling. Report the match win rate of each rung vs the one below on mirrored deals with seat swaps.
findings.detail: Moreno-Montiel numbers: about 31-34% win probability in 4-player individual Mexican rules, where 25% would be the even-chance baseline (my inference).

findings.topic: Capi scoring changes heuristic incentives (pot effect)
findings.claim: Venezuelan and Puerto Rican scoring pays the winner only the losers' pips, so dumping heavy tiles helps only the likely loser. Under Capi, the winning side takes all pips in all hands, partner included. Every tile played therefore shrinks a pot shared by both sides, while the tranque winner is decided by blocker-vs-next-player individual pips.
sources: Capi rules spec in the task prompt (spec, not a source)
https://www.pagat.com/domino/line/partnership.html (Venezuelan and Mexican: winners score only the losers' tiles)
https://acento.com.do/cultura/domino-9463164.html (says only losers' tiles count in the 4-player form)
findings.implication: The prompt must not import 'shed heavy tiles' as a fixed evaluation term from Venezuelan sources. The evaluation and search must use Capi's exact payout and match equity. The engine should discover pot management itself: when likely ahead, avoid shrinking the pot; when likely behind, shrink it, subject to tranque risk.
findings.detail: Sources disagree on scoring. Acento (Dominican) says only the losers' tiles count, while Capi's owner chose all pips including the partner's. Per the owner's rules, Capi's spec governs, and the engine must never 'correct' it.

findings.topic: Evaluation methodology lessons from domino prior art
findings.claim: The credible domino evaluations share one method: mirrored or seat-swapped deals, results pooled across seeds with 95% CIs, a perfect-information oracle as the ceiling, sampler-consistency and never-peeks tests, inference-error counts, calibration of reported probabilities, and head-to-head gating before promoting a new model.
sources: https://github.com/MarAlons0/domino-advisor (Brier-score ProbabilityAnalyzer; backtracking sampler fixed about 2% silent leaks to the real hands)
findings.implication: Write these into the prompt's definition of done. One concrete pitfall: a greedy sampler that dead-ends must fall back to backtracking. 7 Fichas found that about 2% of determinizations silently used the real hidden hands, an information leak, before its v1.2.6 fix.
findings.detail: Single-seed results mislead. fabianruiz3 measured 90.5% at one seed and 84.3% at another for the same configuration, then reported the pooled 87.9%.

findings.topic: 'Dar agua' and other requested terms (verification)
findings.claim: 'Dar agua' is a Cuban table term for shuffling the tiles, not a strategy concept. The UCI thesis says the tiles are mixed, 'o como se dice, darle agua'. An OnCuba column (2014) uses 'mandar a dar agua a los perdedores'. This fits losers shuffling, but that last reading is my inference. 'Pasar con ficha' (Dominican) means passing while holding a playable tile, used figuratively for playing dumb. Capi's must-play rule makes it illegal.
findings.implication: Do not build an engine feature from 'dar agua'. It can appear in UI flavor text only. Terms that are real and documented: salida, salidor, mano, manito, frente, postre, palo/pinta, data (Cuban: a player's tiles of a number), doble en pelo, acompañado, ahorcar, fallo/falla, violín, minga, cuadrar/cuadre, firme, cabeza/encabezado, dekabes, repite, mata, tranque/tranca/trancar, tranco temprano, pase corrido/redondo, pase de salida, capicúa, pollona (Cuban per ASALE via FichaFlow), chuchazo (Puerto Rican), bota gorda, más acompañada, acostarse, negar.
findings.detail: The OnCuba fetch was summarized by a model that read 'dar agua' as a taunt. The thesis definition is explicit, so shuffling is the better-supported meaning.

findings.topic: Test-suite sources: puzzles, annotated games, tournament records
findings.claim: No published collection of dominoes puzzle positions with solutions was found, and no tournament move records either. FID, FEMUNDO and Dominican championships publish results, not games. The usable published material is the three Parra & Trucco deals, the worked examples on dominoarteociencia, the EFDeportes drill types, and the proprietary 'Mesas Didácticas' on JuegoDomino.com, which cannot be reused.
findings.implication: The engine project should generate its own test suite: (1) rules-oracle fixtures from published deals and property tests, (2) solver-verified positions, meaning hidden-information positions whose answer stays the same across all consistent deals, so it is provably correct, (3) soft book-agreement positions from expert rules, (4) later, positions from Capi's own logged games annotated by strong Dominican players. Building such a suite is itself an original contribution.
findings.detail: Books cited by sources but not accessed: Miguel Lugo, 'Competitive Dominoes: How to Play Like a Champion' (Sterling, 1998; Spanish 'Domino Competitivo', AuthorHouse 2008/2009). Miguel Delgado, 'Dominó sin barreras' (Editorial CEC, 2006). Works by Ignacio Zaibert, Héctor Simosa Alarcón, Luis Daniel Balestrini and Alfredo Fernández Porras. Mario Llorente Leyva, 'Dominó: juego y ciencia' (Cuba, EcuRed).

open_questions: The full text of Smith 1973 (CACM) was not accessible (ACM returned 403). Its opponents and tournament format behind 'two-thirds wins, defeated championship players' are unknown.

The engines inside commercial apps (JuegoDomino.com AI review, Capicúa 'Don Capicúa' coach, DR Dominoes, RDomino) are closed. Their real strength is unknown. A direct match against them (manual play vs Capi's engine) is the only way to find out.

No Dominican-authored strategy book or annotated-game collection was found online. The Venezuelan-school sources (Zaibert, Simosa Alarcón, Lugo) are known only through secondary summaries on dominoarteociencia. The owner may know Dominican clubs or champions who could annotate positions.

Sources disagree on Dominican scoring (Acento says only the losers' tiles count in 4-player play, while Capi counts all pips including the partner's) and on tranque ties. The engine follows Capi's spec. The analysis UI may need to explain this to players who learned other table rules.

The Capi-rule scores I derived for the three Parra & Trucco deals (immortal game: pase de salida 25 + two pases corridos 50 + domino 123; tranque deals 126 and 126+25) must be checked by running packages/engine. They are my calculations, not published values.
No human-strength benchmark exists outside Capi. 'Beats elite humans' needs a plan for logged games against strong Dominican players on Capi, with enough games for a CI, since deal variance is high.

Google Play listing details (downloads, update dates) could not be read with WebFetch (truncated pages). App figures come from search snippets and App Store pages that show month and day without the year.

lanes.summary: Recommendation (not fact): write the engine core in Rust as one dependency-light crate with 28-bit u32 hand masks and no allocation in the hot loop. Compile it two ways: a native binary for self-play and benchmarks (rayon across cores), and wasm32 for the Next.js server and the browser. For v1, run every Capi bot on the server (one endpoint used by both web and mobile), and run post-game analysis either in that same server function or in the browser through a Web Worker. Do not put a native engine on the device yet. Measured fact (direct, my own domino playout benchmark on an Apple M1, identical checksums in every runtime): native C ran 1.8M to 2.2M random 2v2 rounds per second on one core, wasm in V8 ran at 0.63x to 0.70x of that, wasm in JavaScriptCore at 0.93x to 0.95x, and carefully written int32/typed-array JS in V8 ran at 0.68x to 0.72x, the same as wasm. The Hermes build that ships with RN 0.76.9 (Capi's pinned version) ran the same JS at only 28.8k to 38.5k rounds per second, about 1/40 of V8 and 1/60 of native, because Hermes has no JIT. Capi's current immutable reducer reached 47k rounds/s on Node and 4.3k/s on Hermes. The bitmask rewrite is therefore 33x faster on Node and 9x faster on Hermes, so the reducer must stay the rules oracle and never sit in a search loop. For RN 0.76, Hermes has no WebAssembly global (facebook/hermes issue #429 is still open). Capi's mobile app also runs the legacy architecture (newArchEnabled false), which rules out Polygen (New Architecture only, 0.2.1 from March 2025) and very likely uniffi-bindgen-react-native (Turbo Modules, docs say early development). If an on-device bot is ever needed, the path that fits the pinned stack is a local Expo module that calls a Rust static library through a C ABI or uniffi Swift/Kotlin bindings. Capi has no expo-updates, so every mobile change already ships as a store build. The real constraint is the pinned-stack rule, not the need for a native rebuild. Vercel in 2026 (fluid compute) supports wasm in Node functions with a 300 s maximum on Hobby (800 s on Pro), 2 GB/1 vCPU on Hobby (up to 4 GB/2 vCPU on Pro), and bills Active CPU at $0.128 per CPU-hour in iad1. One caveat: the Hobby plan is for non-commercial use only, and Capi has ads and in-app purchases. A two-implementation design (TS rules plus Rust engine) needs a differential test harness that treats the TS reducer as the oracle, and the engine prompt should require it. The benchmarks ran on a shared M1 that other lanes were loading (load average 51 to 87), so the ratios are reliable but the absolute numbers are lower bounds. No task-observer observations were logged by this lane (no skill was loaded).

findings.topic: Measured domino playout speed by runtime (Q1, Q4)
findings.claim: On one Apple M1 core, a 2v2 Dominican random-playout loop with bitmask state ran at 1.82M to 2.23M rounds/s native C, 0.63x to 0.70x of that as wasm in V8 (Node 22), 0.93x to 0.95x as wasm in JavaScriptCore (Bun 1.4.1), and 0.68x to 0.72x as int32/typed-array JS in V8. All runtimes produced the same checksum.
findings.detail: Benchmark: first round of a 2v2 deal with the 6-6 placed automatically, uniform random legal moves, tranque detected when no tile outside the board fits, domino and tranque scoring, xorshift32 RNG, checksum 1480882205 in every runtime. Session 1, two runs each, 2,000,000 rounds: c-native (clang 21 -O3 -mcpu=apple-m1) 2,129,905 and 2,226,968 rounds/s; wasm32 (clang -O3) in Bun/JSC 2,063,958 and 2,100,173; JS in Bun 1,429,593 and 1,742,160; JS in Node 22.23.1 1,554,002 and 1,596,169; the same .wasm in Node 22 1,488,917 and 1,561,416; Node --jitless 74,814. Session 2, interleaved best of 5 under load average 51 to 87 from other lanes: c-native 1,817,805; Node JS 1,243,781 (0.68x); wasm in Node 1,154,288 (0.63x); Bun JS 1,119,821 (0.62x). The wasm module was 2,858 bytes. The parallel runs (4 processes: 3.69M aggregate, 8 processes: 4.97M aggregate) were distorted by machine load and should not be used for scaling claims.
findings.implication: The engine prompt should require a playout benchmark with a cross-runtime checksum from day one, report rounds per second with the machine and core count, and plan for wasm in V8 to run about 1.5x slower than native. A TS port can match wasm on a V8 server but can never reach native speed for self-play.

findings.topic: Hermes (RN 0.76) speed for an on-device TS engine (Q3, Q4)
findings.claim: The Hermes VM that ships with Capi's react-native 0.76.9 ran the identical bitmask JS at 38,369 to 38,546 rounds/s (session 1) and 28,777 best of 5 (session 2). That is about 1/40 of V8 JIT and 1/58 to 1/63 of native C.
findings.detail: The binary was node_modules/react-native/sdks/hermesc/osx-bin/hermes, version hermes-2024-11-12-RNv0.76.2, running bytecode compiled with hermesc -O. This is the macOS CLI build, not the iOS framework. Recent iPhones score near an M1 on single core (M1 MacBook Air Geekbench 6 single core is about 2324 to 2375). Mid-range and low-end Android phones are slower; no verified figure was found. The Hermes team removed its JIT experiment (Callstack podcast, secondary), which matches the measured gap. V8 with --jitless (74,814/s) is the closest analogy to an interpreter-only engine.
sources: React Native 0.64 With Hermes for iOS, Callstack podcast (2021) https://callstack.com/podcasts/react-native-0-64-with-hermes-for-ios-ep-5
findings.implication: A TS engine in Hermes gives roughly 20k to 40k random rounds per second of think time on good phones, enough for easy or medium bots but not for elite-strength search. The prompt should not promise elite on-device bots on the current mobile stack.

findings.topic: Current Capi reducer cost in a search loop (Q4)
findings.claim: Random play through Capi's real reducer (createInitialState and applyMove, imported read-only) reached 47,259 rounds/s on Node 22, 68,776 on Bun and 4,303 on Hermes 0.76. The bitmask loop was 33.8x faster on Node, 8.9x faster on Hermes and 47x faster as native C.
findings.detail: Each round is the first round of a 2v2 deal, so the work matches the bitmask benchmark. The reducer copies an immutable GameState and validates every move, so it allocates objects on every move. Bundle: bun build --format=iife, run on Node, Bun and Hermes. The checksum (988318292) matched in all three runtimes.
findings.implication: The prompt must say that packages/engine stays the rules spec and the test oracle, and that search uses its own compact state (u32 masks, two ends, incremental pip sums, pass history) with no allocation per node.

findings.topic: General language speed ratios (Q1)
findings.claim: On CPU benchmarks, Rust and C++ run within about 0.7x to 1.3x of each other. Go is 2x to 13x slower than Rust, Node.js is 2.2x to 28x slower, and Zig is mixed against Rust (roughly equal to 1.9x slower).
findings.detail: Benchmarks Game 25.03, fastest elapsed seconds on a quad-core Intel i5-3330 (Ubuntu 24.04), Rust 1.84.1, g++ 14.2, go1.23.1, Node v23.8.0. Rust vs C++: fannkuch-redux 3.81 vs 3.33, n-body 2.19 vs 2.15, spectral-norm 0.72 vs 0.72, regex-redux 0.78 vs 1.14. Go vs Rust: fannkuch 8.36 vs 3.81 (2.2x), n-body 6.39 vs 2.19 (2.9x), binary-trees 14.21 vs 1.07 (13x). Node vs Rust: fannkuch 11.07 vs 3.81 (2.9x), n-body 8.55 vs 2.19 (3.9x), spectral-norm 1.60 vs 0.72 (2.2x), reverse-complement 15.53 vs 0.55 (28x). Several of the fastest Rust programs use hand-written SIMD or unsafe code, and many programs run multi-core. programming-language-benchmarks (AMD EPYC 7763, 4 cores, 2025-08-01, rustc 1.88, zig 0.14.1): single-thread fannkuch-redux(11) Rust 2700 ms vs Zig 2716 ms, nbody 163 vs 198 ms, single-thread spectral-norm 1964 vs 3687 ms, nsieve 301 vs 267 ms. These are not dominoes, so they are analogy. My domino benchmark shows a smaller JS gap (1.4x to 1.6x) than Benchmarks Game, because the loop uses only 32-bit integers.
sources: Benchmarks Game 25.03, Rust vs C++ g++ (2025) https://benchmarksgame-team.pages.debian.net/benchmarksgame/fastest/rust-gpp.html
Benchmarks Game, how programs are measured (2025) https://benchmarksgame-team.pages.debian.net/benchmarksgame/how-programs-are-measured.html
findings.implication: Choose Rust or C++ for the core. Go has a garbage collector, is 2x to 3x slower on these kernels and produces multi-megabyte wasm. Zig is pre-1.0. Neither suits a long-lived engine that also targets wasm.

findings.topic: WebAssembly vs native (Q1)
findings.claim: On full SPEC CPU applications, wasm ran on average 45% slower (Firefox) and 55% slower (Chrome) than native, with peak slowdowns of 2.08x and 2.5x. On the small domino kernel, wasm reached 0.63x to 0.70x of native in V8 and 0.93x to 0.95x in JavaScriptCore.
findings.detail: Jangda, Powers, Berger, Guha, 'Not So Fast: Analyzing the Performance of WebAssembly vs. Native Code', USENIX ATC 2019. No 2024 to 2026 SPEC-scale replication was found. The kernel results are from this lane's own benchmark. Lichess forum reports on Stockfish wasm vs native are anecdotal and use different hardware, so they are not usable.
findings.implication: Plan for wasm in Node or a browser to deliver about 0.5x to 0.7x of native throughput. Keep the hot loop to 32-bit integer operations, and measure wasm and native builds side by side in CI.

findings.topic: Hermes WebAssembly status (Q3)
findings.claim: Hermes in RN 0.76 has no WebAssembly global. As of 2026, no primary source confirms Wasm execution in any Hermes release.
findings.detail: facebook/hermes issue #429 ('WASM support within Hermes?') is open. Maintainer tmikov (Sep 2024) recommends running wasm2js first and compiling the result with Hermes or Static Hermes, and argues against embedding a Wasm engine. The official React Native 0.84 post (2026-02-11, Hermes V1 by default) does not mention WebAssembly. A Callstack event page (2026-02-19) claims 'WebAssembly support landing in Hermes' with no details; this lane could not verify it. Capi pins RN 0.76.9 and Expo SDK 52, so the question is moot for Capi without a major upgrade.
sources: React Native 0.84 - Hermes V1 by Default (2026-02-11) https://reactnative.dev/blog/2026/02/11/react-native-0.84
Callstack, React Native 0.84: Hermes v1, WebAssembly, and Ecosystem Shifts (2026-02-19) https://www.callstack.com/events/react-native-0-84-and-other-news
findings.implication: The prompt must not plan a wasm engine running inside Hermes on Capi mobile. wasm2js output would run at Hermes interpreter speed, no faster than the 38k rounds/s measured.

findings.topic: React Native wasm and Rust binding libraries vs Capi's legacy architecture (Q3)
findings.claim: Capi's mobile app runs the legacy architecture (newArchEnabled false, Hermes). This blocks Polygen (New Architecture only) and very likely uniffi-bindgen-react-native (Turbo Modules). The other RN wasm libraries are unmaintained.
findings.detail: Facts: ios/Podfile.properties.json has newArchEnabled false. Expo SDK 52 enabled the New Architecture only for new projects. Polygen: npm latest 0.2.1 (2025-03-20), README says 'Only new RN Architecture is supported', RN 0.75+, AOT through wasm2c, no threads, 'still under active development'. uniffi-bindgen-react-native: npm 0.31.0-6 (2026-09-25), repo pushed 2026-10-23, Rust to Turbo Module plus a generated wasm-bindgen crate for web, tutorial tested on RN 0.75 and 0.76 with the 'Turbo module' template, docs say early development and not yet for production. react-native-webassembly 0.3.3 (2023-05-10, wasm3 interpreter); react-native-wasm 0.1.3 (2021-02-17). Inference: the uniffi-bindgen-react-native Turbo Module template needs the New Architecture; its docs do not say so explicitly.
sources: Mozilla Hacks, Introducing Uniffi for React Native (2024-12) https://hacks.mozilla.org/2024/12/introducing-uniffi-for-react-native-rust-powered-turbo-modules/
findings.implication: Any on-device native engine must use the Expo Modules API, which already works in this app on the legacy architecture. Adopting Polygen or uniffi-bindgen-react-native requires Adelson to approve a New Architecture migration first.

findings.topic: On-device paths that fit the pinned mobile stack (Q3)
findings.claim: Three on-device options fit Expo SDK 52 on the legacy architecture: (a) a local Expo module (Swift/Kotlin) that calls a Rust static library through a C ABI or uniffi Swift/Kotlin bindings, running at native speed; (b) TS on a Reanimated worklet runtime off the JS thread, at Hermes speed; (c) an Expo DOM component in a WKWebView running the wasm build with JIT. None of them avoids a store build, and none is needed for v1.
findings.detail: Facts: Capi already ships a local Expo module (apps/mobile/modules/capi-shared, iOS only) on the legacy architecture. Expo AsyncFunction runs native code on a thread other than the JS runtime by default. The installed react-native-reanimated 3.16.7 exports createWorkletRuntime and runOnRuntime, which run worklets on a separate thread. Expo SDK 52 introduced DOM components, which need react-native-webview on SDK 55 and earlier and pass data over an async JSON bridge. WKWebView runs JavaScriptCore out of process with JIT, while in-process JSContext has no JIT (older sources, 2015 to 2019). apps/mobile/package.json has no expo-updates, so every JS change already ships as a store build. uniffi 0.32.2 (2026-09-23) is active. Inference, unverified: workletizing a whole engine on Reanimated 3 (every function needs the 'worklet' directive) and calling runOnJS from a custom worklet runtime both need a spike before anyone relies on them.
findings.implication: Defer on-device bots. If Adelson later wants offline bots, the prompt should specify a local Expo module that wraps a prebuilt Rust staticlib or xcframework and Android .so files, so EAS builds need no Rust toolchain.

findings.topic: Vercel limits and pricing for a server-side engine, 2026 (Q2, Q3)
findings.claim: With fluid compute, Vercel Node functions run up to 300 s on Hobby (default and maximum) and up to 800 s on Pro (1800 s in beta). Memory and CPU are 2 GB/1 vCPU on Hobby and up to 4 GB/2 vCPU on Pro. Active CPU costs $0.128 per CPU-hour in iad1, and Hobby is restricted to non-commercial use.
findings.detail: Limits page (last updated 2026-08-24): bundle 250 MB uncompressed (large functions up to 5 GB in beta), payload 4.5 MB, default region iad1. Pricing page (2026-06-16): iad1 Active CPU $0.128/h, provisioned memory $0.0106/GB-h. Hobby includes 4 CPU-hours, 360 GB-hours and 1M invocations per month. Pro invocations cost $0.60 per million. The Wasm docs page (2025-12-08) says Wasm works in the edge, nodejs and bun runtimes, but Edge only accepts Wasm through a static import with no buffer compile. The Rust runtime is in Beta on all plans. The Hobby plan page (2026-09-14) says Hobby is for non-commercial, personal use only. Capi shows ads and sells in-app purchases.
findings.implication: Run the engine as wasm in a Next.js route with runtime nodejs (not edge), set an explicit maxDuration, and give each request a fixed CPU-time budget. Flag the plan question (Hobby is non-commercial and includes only 4 CPU-hours per month) to Adelson before launching bots.

findings.topic: Rust to wasm in the Next.js 14 web app (Q2)
findings.claim: Next.js 14 with webpack 5 loads wasm once experiments.asyncWebAssembly is enabled (official with-webassembly example). Browser search can run in Web Workers with one wasm instance per worker. Shared-memory wasm threads would need nightly Rust plus cross-origin isolation, which Safari supports only through COEP require-corp.
findings.detail: The Next.js example's next.config.js sets config.experiments.asyncWebAssembly = true and a webassemblyModuleFilename for server builds. wasm-bindgen-rayon README: threads need nightly Rust (tested nightly-2025-11-15), +atomics,+bulk-memory, build-std, and cross-origin isolation. MDN: SharedArrayBuffer needs crossOriginIsolated, set with COOP same-origin plus COEP require-corp or credentialless. MDN compatibility data: COEP credentialless works in Chrome 96 and Firefox 119 but not in Safari, and require-corp blocks cross-origin no-cors resources that lack a CORP header. Capi's next.config.js sets no COOP or COEP headers today. A third-party guide reports that a literal new Worker(new URL(...)) can crash under some Next.js setups; that report is secondary. Bundle size: the domino kernel compiled to 2,858 bytes of wasm (measured). A full engine with wasm-bindgen glue was not measured.
findings.implication: The prompt should forbid wasm threads and SharedArrayBuffer in v1, use stable Rust, and parallelize browser analysis with N independent Workers (root parallelism over determinizations). No COOP or COEP headers are then needed, so other site features are not affected.

findings.topic: Rust wasm toolchain maintenance (Q2, Q5)
findings.claim: The rustwasm GitHub org was sunset in 2025. wasm-bindgen and wasm-pack now live in the wasm-bindgen org and are actively released.
findings.detail: Inside Rust blog (2025-07-21): wasm-bindgen moved to a new org with additional maintainers, and other repos were archived or handed to their existing maintainers. crates.io API (queried 2026-10-25): wasm-bindgen 0.2.129, updated 2026-09-25, repo github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-bindgen, 157.8M downloads in the last 90 days. wasm-pack 0.15.0, updated 2026-05-15, repo github.com/wasm-bindgen/wasm-pack. js-sys and web-sys 0.3.106 (2026-09-25). The Rust and WebAssembly book is reported as unmaintained (community forum, secondary).
sources: Inside Rust, Sunsetting the rustwasm GitHub org (2025-07-21) https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2025/07/21/sunsetting-the-rustwasm-github-org
findings.implication: Use wasm-bindgen with wasm-pack (or wasm-bindgen-cli) from the wasm-bindgen org, and pin their versions. Do not follow the old rustwasm book templates.

findings.topic: Alternative server hosts: limits and small-scale cost (Q3)
findings.claim: Supabase Edge Functions cap CPU at 2 s per request with 256 MB of memory. Cloudflare Workers Paid allows up to 5 min of CPU per request with 128 MB per isolate for $5/month including 30M CPU-ms. Fly shared CPUs have a 1/16-core baseline, and a dedicated core costs $33/month. Render's free tier spins down after 15 minutes of inactivity.
findings.detail: Supabase limits page: 256 MB, 2 s CPU per request (async I/O excluded), wall clock 150 s on Free and 400 s on paid, 20 MB function size through the CLI. The Wasm guide uses wasm-pack --target deno and static_files (CLI 2.7.0 or later). Invocation quota is 500k on Free and 2M on Pro; the $2 per extra million figure is from a secondary source. Cloudflare limits page (2026-10-12): Free 10 ms CPU per request; Paid default 30 s CPU, up to 5 min; 128 MB per isolate including Wasm memory; 64 MiB uncompressed script. Pricing page (2026-10-02): $5/month minimum, 10M requests and 30M CPU-ms included, then $0.30 per million requests and $0.02 per million CPU-ms. Fly: shared-cpu-1x 512 MB costs $3.69/month and performance-1x 2 GB costs $33.00/month; stopped machines bill only rootfs; shared vCPU baseline is 1/16 core with a burst balance. Render: free services spin down after 15 minutes with about a 1 minute cold start; Starter is $7/month for 512 MB and 0.5 CPU (secondary sources, because the official pricing page did not render).
findings.implication: Supabase Edge is too tight for a fixed 1 to 2 s search per move, because the 2 s CPU cap includes all request overhead. Vercel (already hosting Capi's API) or Cloudflare Workers are the serverless options. A small dedicated VM is the fallback if wasm throughput or the CPU cap becomes the limit.

findings.topic: Cost arithmetic for server bots at small scale (Q3)
findings.claim: For 90,000 bot moves per month at 1 CPU-second each (25 CPU-hours), the compute cost is about $3.80 on Vercel Pro in iad1, $6.20 on Cloudflare Workers Paid including the $5 base, and $0 extra on Supabase Edge within plan quotas.
findings.detail: Basis: 1,000 bot games per month, up to 3 bot seats, about 30 moves per bot seat per game. Vercel Pro iad1: 25 CPU-h x $0.128 = $3.20, plus memory 2 GB x 1.1 s x 90,000 / 3600 = 55 GB-h x $0.0106 = $0.58, plus invocations $0.05. The Pro seat is $20/month on top. Hobby includes 4 CPU-hours, which covers only 14,400 one-second moves. Cloudflare: 90M CPU-ms minus 30M included = 60M x $0.02/M = $1.20, plus $5. Supabase: 90k invocations fit inside the Free (500k) or Pro (2M) quota, and CPU is not billed separately but is capped at 2 s per request. Fly shared-cpu-1x: a 1/16-core baseline gives about 162,000 CPU-s per month before throttling, so the load fits only if it stays bursty. One CPU-second is not the same amount of work on every provider, and no provider's CPU speed was measured.
findings.implication: Cost does not decide the hosting choice at Capi's scale. The prompt should make per-move CPU budget a configuration value and log CPU milliseconds per bot move so the real cost can be measured.

findings.topic: Crates and frameworks for game search (Q5)
findings.claim: No widely used, maintained Rust crate exists for MCTS or ISMCTS. The supporting crates for parallelism, benchmarking, testing, bindings and ML are all actively maintained. OpenSpiel has dominoes games, but only in Python.
findings.detail: crates.io API, 2026-10-25: mcts 0.3.0 (last updated 2019-03-09, 11,303 downloads); ismcts 0.3.3 (2025-06-24, 5,883 downloads); mcts-rs 0.1.0 (2024-10-22, 1,315); treant 0.4.0 (2026-04-14, 685); cfr 0.6.2 (2026-09-02, 15,225). Active: rayon 1.12.0 (2026-04-14), criterion 0.8.2 (2026-02-04), proptest 1.12.0 (2026-10-10), pyo3 0.30.1 (2026-10-14), maturin 1.15.0 (2026-08-27), uniffi 0.32.2 (2026-09-23), napi 3.15.0 (2026-10-22), burn 0.22.1 (2026-10-20), candle-core 0.11.0 (2026-06-26), ort 2.0.0-rc.15 (2026-10-19). OpenSpiel (Apache-2.0, v2.0.2 released 2026-08-12, repo pushed 2026-10-25) lists Block Dominoes (2 players) and Team Dominoes (4 players) as imperfect-information games marked 'implemented but lightly tested'. Both are pure Python (open_spiel/python/games/block_dominoes.py and team_dominoes.py), and their rules are not Capi's rules.
sources: crates.io API, crate pages for mcts, ismcts, rayon, criterion, proptest, pyo3, uniffi, napi, burn, candle-core, ort (queried 2026-10-25) https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/
findings.implication: The prompt should have the engine implement its own search (determinized or information-set MCTS) on top of rayon, criterion and proptest. OpenSpiel is useful only as an algorithm reference or a sanity-check opponent, not as a runtime or a rules source.

findings.topic: Developer experience and resume value (Q5)
findings.claim: Facts: Rust was the most admired language in the 2025 Stack Overflow survey (72%), with Zig at 64%. Zig is still pre-1.0 (0.17.0 released 2026-10-01) and introduces breaking changes in each minor release. Go wasm binaries are measured in megabytes. Assessment: one Rust core that builds for native, wasm (server and browser) and possibly mobile, with a benchmark suite and a differential test against a TS oracle, is a stronger systems-engineering story than a TS-only engine.
findings.detail: Stack Overflow 2025 technology page: Rust 72% admired, Gleam 70%, Elixir 66%, Zig 64%. ziglang.org download index: 0.16.0 (2026-04-13), 0.17.0 (2026-10-01), master 0.18.0-dev. Secondary reports call 0.16 heavily breaking (new std.Io). Go: a 2019 GopherCon talk reports a 1.37 MB hello-world wasm without fmt, while TinyGo builds are about 100x smaller. AssemblyScript 0.28.20 (2026-07-22) is a TS-like wasm option, but it would still be a second implementation of the rules, without Rust's tooling or its native target. The resume-value statement is an inference, not a measured fact.
sources: Sourcegraph, GopherCon 2019 Get Going with WebAssembly (2019) https://sourcegraph.com/blog/go/gophercon-2019-get-going-with-webassembly
findings.implication: The prompt should use stable Rust and present the project as a multi-target engine: native self-play runner, wasm in a Vercel function, wasm in a browser Web Worker. It should include published benchmarks (rounds/s, nodes/s, Elo or win rate with N games) as resume-grade artifacts.

findings.topic: Rules parity with two implementations (Q4, Q5)
findings.claim: A Rust core creates a second implementation of Capi's rules. A differential test harness that uses Capi's TS reducer as the oracle is required.
findings.detail: The TS reducer already runs at 47k rounds/s on Node, fast enough to replay millions of seeded random games in Vitest against the Rust engine loaded as wasm, comparing legal-move sets, ends, passes, pase corrido, pase de salida, capicua, tranque winner and scores step by step. Without such a harness, a rules drift would silently corrupt bot play and analysis. A TS-only engine avoids the problem but caps self-play and server throughput at JS speed and on-device speed at Hermes speed.
findings.implication: The prompt should make the differential test a release gate: N seeded games (for example 1,000,000) per mode (1v1 with boneyard, 2v2) with zero mismatches, run in CI against the wasm build.

findings.topic: Where bots must run in Capi's architecture (Q3)
findings.claim: Capi's server is authoritative and Capi has no AI or offline play today. Bots seated in online games therefore have to run server-side, and the mobile bot and the web bot can be the same server bot.
findings.detail: PLAYBOOK: both clients use the same Next.js API on Vercel plus Supabase. Game state is a single GameState JSON row with optimistic concurrency. The 'Never claim' list includes AI opponents, solo play and offline play (Capi's own docs describe architecture, not rules). Inference: a server bot must receive only its information set (own hand, board, play and pass history, hand counts), never the full GameState, so it cannot see hidden hands by accident. Bot think time of 0.5 to 2 s is also a game-feel choice, so network round-trip time is small next to it.
findings.implication: The engine API should take an observation or information-set type, not GameState. The prompt should specify one server bot endpoint for both clients and leave on-device bots out of scope.

findings.topic: Recommendation matrix (all questions)
findings.claim: Recommendation, not fact: Rust core; native Rust self-play and benchmark runner; analysis service as Rust-to-wasm in a Next.js nodejs route on Vercel; web bot and mobile bot both served by that server endpoint; browser-side wasm in Web Workers only for the analysis UI.
findings.detail: Engine core: Rust stable, one crate with no I/O, u32 masks, fixed-size arrays, a seeded RNG and no allocation in the hot loop. Build targets: native and wasm32-unknown-unknown. Self-play and benchmark runner: native binary with rayon, criterion, a checksum benchmark and the differential-test harness. Add PyO3 and maturin only if a PyTorch value network is added later. Run on the M1 or a cloud VM. Analysis service: wasm loaded once per instance in a runtime nodejs route, with a per-request CPU budget and maxDuration at or below 300 s (Hobby) or 800 s (Pro). Expected wasm-in-V8 speed is 0.63x to 0.70x of native, as measured. Fallbacks if throughput is short: napi-rs native addon, the Vercel Rust runtime (Beta) or a dedicated VM. Capi web bot: server-side for online tables (authority, fairness, bots keep playing when a client disconnects); a client wasm Web Worker for post-game analysis, without threads, SharedArrayBuffer or COOP/COEP. Capi mobile bot: the same server API in v1. Later on-device option: a local Expo module that wraps a prebuilt Rust staticlib (legacy-architecture compatible). TS-in-Hermes is suitable only for easy bots. Polygen and uniffi-bindgen-react-native need a New Architecture migration that Adelson must approve first.
findings.implication: Use this matrix as the deployment section of the engine-build prompt, and label each row as a recommendation that rests on the facts above.

open_questions: Which Vercel plan is Capi on? Hobby is restricted to non-commercial use, caps functions at 300 s and includes only 4 Active CPU-hours per month. Capi shows ads and sells in-app purchases.
Which Supabase plan and region does Capi use, and is the Vercel function region (default iad1) co-located with it?
Does Adelson want offline or solo bots on mobile? PLAYBOOK.md:104 currently forbids claiming AI opponents, solo play or offline play, and that decides whether any on-device engine is in scope.
Is a New Architecture migration of apps/mobile on the table? It is the only way to use Polygen or uniffi-bindgen-react-native, and it is a pinned-stack decision.

Benchmarks ran on a shared M1 with load average 51 to 87 from other lanes. Ratios agreed across two sessions, but absolute rounds/s should be rerun on an idle machine, and Hermes should be measured on a real iPhone and on mid-range and low-end Android phones.

The claim that WebAssembly support landed in Hermes with RN 0.84 comes only from a Callstack event page (2026-02-19). The official RN 0.84 post does not mention it. This lane could not verify it, and it does not affect Capi on RN 0.76.
