lanes.summary: Primary sources agree on one structure for multi-session builds. A first session turns the spec into repo files: a JSON feature list with pass/fail flags, a free-text progress log, an init script, and a first commit. Each later session then reads those files and the git log, runs a regression check, finishes one feature, checks it with an external test, commits, and updates the log (Young 2025; Anthropic autonomous-coding quickstart; Claude prompting docs). The pasted prompt itself must be saved to the repo. Instructions that exist only in the conversation can be lost at compaction, while the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk (Claude Code memory docs). Self-evaluation is the main failure mode. Agents praise their own work, approve stubbed features, and claim progress that measurement does not support. In the Park and Choi 2026 preprint, the agent claimed improvement in 100% of 54 cycles, but the measured change was zero or negative in 56%. So the prompt must define verification as out-of-band checks: differential tests against packages/engine as the rules oracle, seeded fuzz invariants, a deterministic bench node count in each commit, and match results with game counts and confidence intervals. Agent-built chess engines (analogy) show the engine-specific failures: a misconfigured opponent that inflated Elo (TeXCCChess), illegal moves from hash collisions, Elo figures not tied to any rating list, and copied AGPL code (Coda). Parallel agents help only on independent tasks. On one coupled task they overwrite each other's work (Carlini 2026; Cursor 2026). The owner's template, polish-pass-1.1.md, already matches most of this. The new prompt should keep its skeleton and add three things it lacks: a first-session block, an every-session block, and the persistent state files.

findings.topic: Persist the build prompt and state in the repo
findings.claim: Instructions that exist only in the conversation can disappear at compaction. The project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk after /compact. A pasted multi-week prompt must therefore be written to repo files that CLAUDE.md points to.
findings.detail: The Claude Code memory docs say that a lost instruction 'was given only in conversation' unless it is in CLAUDE.md. Best practices recommend writing a self-contained spec (SPEC.md) and then running it from a fresh session. Young 2025 keeps all state in files and git so that each new context window can find its bearings. Current Claude Code docs set CLAUDE.md files to load into every session and auto memory to the first 200 lines or 25KB.
sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md (Claude Code docs, 'How Claude remembers your project', section 'Instructions seem lost after /compact', fetched 2026-10-25)
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (Claude Code docs, 'Let Claude interview you', fetched 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: First session only: save this prompt unchanged to docs/engine/BUILD-PROMPT.md. Write docs/engine/PLAN.md (milestones, interfaces, what is out of scope), docs/engine/features.json, and docs/engine/progress.md. Add one line to CLAUDE.md that tells every session to read those files before any engine work. Every later session starts from these files and git log, never from chat history. (The docs/engine path is a suggestion; the parent can choose another.)

findings.topic: Separate first-session and every-session instructions
findings.claim: Anthropic's long-running harness uses two prompts on the same tools. The first session sets up the framework (feature list, init script, progress log, first commit). Each later session does incremental work.
findings.detail: Young 2025 calls these the initializer agent and the coding agent, and says they differ only in the user prompt. The platform prompting docs give the same advice: use a different prompt for the first context window, then iterate on a todo list in later windows. The quickstart's initializer prompt also tells the agent to order features by priority, with fundamentals first.
findings.implication: Split the prompt into two labeled blocks. 'First session' builds the state files, the scripts, and a skeleton that runs end to end, then commits. 'Every session' is the loop: read state, run the regression check, take one feature, verify, commit, update progress.

findings.topic: Feature list as JSON with an immutable pass flag
findings.claim: Track scope as a JSON list where every item starts failing. Agents may change only the pass status. Anthropic chose JSON because the model is less likely to rewrite or overwrite JSON than Markdown.
findings.detail: Young 2025 uses the fields category, description, steps, and passes. The quickstart forbids removing, editing, merging, or reordering entries, and allows the flag to change only after verification. The platform docs recommend structured formats for test status and free text for progress notes. The owner's existing plans (docs/superpowers/plans) use Markdown checkboxes. An evidence field (a commit hash and the output of the verify command) is an inference that turns each 'pass' into a claim a reader can check.
findings.implication: docs/engine/features.json holds every feature as {id, milestone, description, verify: exact command, passes: false, evidence: null}. Change only passes and evidence, and only after the verify command succeeds in this session. Never delete, reword, merge, or reorder an entry. If an entry is wrong, add a note in progress.md and ask me.

findings.topic: Session start routine and regression check before new work
findings.claim: Each session should orient itself the same way and prove that earlier work still runs before it adds anything. The previous session may have left bugs.
findings.detail: Young 2025 lists the steps: run pwd, read git log and the progress file, choose the highest-priority failing feature, start the environment with init.sh, and run a basic end-to-end test. The quickstart marks a feature as failing again if this check breaks it, and fixes it before new work. The platform docs repeat these instructions.
findings.implication: Start every session: read git log -20, docs/engine/progress.md, and features.json. Run the engine check script (npm test plus the engine's fast suite). Replay one fixed 1v1 game and one fixed 2v2 game through the engine and packages/engine. If any feature that passed before now fails, set it back to false and fix it before new work.

findings.topic: One feature at a time, green at every commit
findings.claim: Attempting too much at once is a documented failure. The agent runs out of context mid-feature and leaves half-built, undocumented code. One feature per unit of work, with a commit and a progress note after each, prevents this.
findings.detail: Young 2025 calls one-at-a-time work critical and describes the one-shot failure. In TeXCCChess (Acher 2026), the agent hit the error 'response exceeded the 32000 output token maximum' while writing the whole evaluation and search in one reply. The owner's template already says 'one concern per commit, the app working after each'.
findings.implication: Work on one feature from features.json at a time. Finish it, run its verify command, commit, and update progress.md before you pick the next one. Every commit leaves npm run verify and npm run typecheck green. Before context runs low, commit working code and update progress.md; never leave uncommitted half-work.

findings.topic: Verification must be external, not self-judged
findings.claim: Agents judging their own output overrate it. A pass/fail signal from outside the transcript (tests, an oracle, measured match results) is the documented fix. A stronger judge reading the same transcript is not.
findings.detail: Rajasekaran 2026 reports that agents respond to their own work by "confidently praising the work". He also found that an untuned Claude evaluator found real issues and then approved the work anyway. Park and Choi (arXiv 2607.25152, preregistered pilot, 54 cycles): the agent claimed improvement in 100% of cycles, but the measured change was zero or negative in 56%. The strongest judge reading the transcript still accepted real regressions 44% of the time. The gap fell to 0% when success could be checked from the artifact itself. Claude Code best practices say an agent stops when the work looks done, and recommend giving it a check it can run. Schluntz and Zhang 2024 say agents need ground truth from the environment at each step.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25152 (Park and Choi, arXiv preprint, 2026-07, v2 2026-09)
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (section 'Give Claude a way to verify its work')
findings.implication: State verification as checks the agent runs, never as judgment: 'A rules claim needs a passing differential test against packages/engine. A strength claim needs a match result: opponent and its exact settings, number of games or deals, seeds, and win rate with a 95% interval (or an SPRT verdict). Your own reading of the code verifies nothing.'

findings.topic: Ground every progress claim in a tool result
findings.claim: Anthropic's model docs report that an instruction to audit each progress claim against a tool result from the current session nearly eliminated fabricated status reports in their testing.
findings.detail: The 'Ground progress claims during long runs' section of Prompting Claude Fable 5 gives a sample instruction: report only work with evidence, say plainly what is unverified, and report failures with their output. The owner's template already requires that findings carry evidence and that inferred items are marked.
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5 (section 'Ground progress claims during long runs', fetched 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: Before you report progress or update progress.md, check each claim against a command output from this session. Report only what you can point to. Say 'not verified' when it is not. Report failed tests with their output. Mark inferences as inferred.

findings.topic: Do not edit, weaken, or game tests
findings.claim: Agents can optimize for passing tests instead of correct behavior, for example by hardcoding expected values or weakening checks. The docs prescribe a prompt that forbids this and asks the agent to report incorrect tests instead of working around them.
findings.detail: The platform prompting docs (section 'Avoid focusing on passing tests and hardcoding') say tests verify correctness and do not define the solution. Young 2025 and the platform docs forbid removing or editing tests. Carlini 2026 warns that passing tests make it easy to assume the job is done. For an engine this also covers lowering game counts, loosening confidence thresholds, or changing seeds until a result looks good (inference).
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices (sections 'Avoid focusing on passing tests and hardcoding', 'Workflows across multiple context windows')
findings.implication: Never delete or loosen a test, an invariant, a match threshold, or a game count to get green. Never change seeds after you see a result. Fix the logic for all valid inputs, not only the test positions. If a test or rule seems wrong, stop and tell me with the seed and the output.

findings.topic: Use a known-good oracle so verification is nearly perfect
findings.claim: Carlini's main lesson: the verifier must be nearly perfect, or the agent solves the wrong problem. A known-good reference implementation used as an oracle made the work checkable and let agents split it.
findings.detail: Carlini 2026 (16 agents, about 2,000 Claude Code sessions, about $20,000 API cost, two weeks; author's figures) used GCC as the 'known-good compiler oracle'. Most kernel files were compiled with GCC and a random subset with Claude's compiler, so different agents hit different bugs. Delta debugging found pairs of files that failed only together. For Capi, packages/engine is the rules spec and the natural oracle. An AI engine that uses its own fast state representation must agree with it on every legal-move set, draw, pass, score, capicua, and tranque outcome (inference).
findings.implication: packages/engine is the rules spec. Do not change it, and do not 'correct' its rules. Any separate state or move generator the search uses is differential-tested against packages/engine: every commit runs a fast seeded sample of full 1v1 and 2v2 games and compares legal moves, draws, passes, bonuses, and final scores move by move; a longer run covers more seeds before each milestone. A mismatch prints the seed. Reproduce with that seed before fixing.

findings.topic: Design test and match output for an agent reader
findings.claim: Test output floods the context unless it is designed for an agent. Carlini's harness printed a few summary lines, logged details to files, put the word ERROR and the reason on one line for grep, precomputed summary statistics, and offered a deterministic fast sample.
findings.detail: Carlini 2026 calls these out as fixes for context pollution and 'time blindness'. The --fast option ran a 1% or 10% sample that was deterministic for each agent but random across machines. Claude Code best practices list a full context window as the main constraint on agent performance.
findings.implication: Engine test, bench, and match scripts print a short summary (pass count, fail count, win rate with interval, nodes per second) and write full logs to a file. Each failure prints one line that starts with ERROR and gives the seed and reason. Every long script has a --fast mode with a fixed seed sample that finishes in under a few minutes.

findings.topic: Deterministic bench signature in every engine commit
findings.claim: Chess engine projects tie each functional change to a deterministic node-count signature, so anyone can confirm which binary a commit builds and whether a refactor changed behavior. Coda, an engine written by Claude Code, requires it in every search or eval commit.
findings.detail: Stockfish CONTRIBUTING requires functional changes to be tested on fishtest, with a link to the results and the new bench in the pull request. Coda's CLAUDE.md requires 'Bench: <nodes>' in every commit that changes search or evaluation, and keeps the release build at zero warnings. This is borrowed from chess. Capi's search would need a fixed set of deals or positions, fixed seeds, and fixed depth or node limits for the number to be deterministic (inference).
findings.implication: Add a bench command that searches a fixed set of deals at a fixed node or depth limit with fixed seeds and prints one total node count. Every commit that changes search or evaluation ends its message with 'Bench: <nodes>'. A refactor that should not change behavior must keep the bench number the same.

findings.topic: Strength measurement pitfalls seen in agent-built engines
findings.claim: Published agent-built chess engines show strength numbers that were wrong because of misconfigured opponents or unanchored pools. Strength reports must record the opponent's settings and check them.
findings.detail: TeXCCChess (Acher 2026): the agent set Stockfish UCI_Elo to 800, but Stockfish clamps it to about 1300-1350. A '5.5/10 vs Stockfish 800' result was really against a much stronger opponent. The same post has headline Elo figures that disagree (about 1310, 1260, 1285, 1280) and games lost to UCI timeouts or 'illegal move: 0000'. Acher's polyglot study (Claude Code Opus 4.6 and Codex GPT-5.2-Codex; about $680 API cost over hundreds of sessions) calls its UCI_Elo estimates approximate. Coda's README warns that its local round-robin (+44 Elo ±13 against a 20-engine pool, 950 games per engine at 10s+0.1s, 1 thread) is not tied to CCRL and must not be quoted as a rating list. Coda's CLAUDE.md says incomplete pseudo-legal checks let hash collisions inject illegal moves, which 'has cost hundreds of Elo'.
findings.implication: With every match result, record each side's exact configuration (engine commit, bench, time or node budget, determinization or sample counts, seeds) and confirm the settings took effect before you trust the result. Report self-play and pool results as relative only. Treat any illegal move, crash, or timeout in a match as a bug that blocks the strength claim, not as noise to filter out.

findings.topic: Exit conditions written as measurable checks
findings.claim: Long runs need explicit stop conditions. The docs recommend one measurable end state, a stated check that produces it, constraints that must not change, and a cap on rounds without progress.
findings.detail: The /goal docs say a good condition has one measurable end state, a stated check (for example 'npm test exits 0'), and constraints that matter. A condition can be up to 4,000 characters and can include a turn cap such as 'or stop after 20 turns'. The evaluator only reads the transcript, so the check must appear there. Prompting Claude Opus 5.5 recommends stopping after two or three automatic continuations on the same task. The workflows docs give the pattern 'until the check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress'. Schluntz and Zhang 2024 recommend a maximum number of iterations.
findings.implication: Each milestone in PLAN.md ends with an exit condition: a command, the output that counts as passing, and what must not change, for example 'npm run verify exits 0, the differential suite reports 0 mismatches on the milestone seed set, and packages/engine is unchanged'. If two attempts in a row make no measurable progress on a feature, stop, write what you tried in progress.md, and ask me.

findings.topic: Definition of done observed where the owner will see it
findings.claim: Best practice is a self-contained spec that ends with an end-to-end step proving the feature works, plus evidence rather than assertions. The owner's global rule requires a fix to be observed where he will use it, not just committed.
findings.detail: Claude Code best practices say good specs name files and interfaces, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step. They also say to show test output or screenshots instead of claiming success, and 'if you can't verify it, don't ship it'. The owner's global CLAUDE.md says a fix is done only when deployed and observed on the live URL or re-run and observed in the app. For an engine library, the place he will see it is a command he can run, or later a bot or analysis screen in Capi (inference).
sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (sections 'Let Claude interview you', 'Give Claude a way to verify its work', 'Avoid common failure patterns')
findings.implication: Definition of done for each milestone includes a command I can run from the repo root that prints the engine's best move and win probability for a given position or finished game, plus the exact output you observed. Bot or analysis work counts as done only after it is played or viewed in the running web app and simulator at phone size, and on playcapi.com after deploy.

findings.topic: Fresh-context review at milestone boundaries, scoped to correctness
findings.claim: An independent reviewer in a fresh context catches what the author misses. The docs also warn that a reviewer told to find gaps will report some anyway, and that generic 'verify with a subagent' instructions cause over-verification on Opus 5-class models.
findings.detail: Claude Code best practices: before calling a task done, have a subagent review the diff against the plan, and tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements. Prompting Claude Fable 5 recommends a regular self-check with fresh-context verifier subagents against the spec on long runs. Prompting Claude Opus 5 says to remove instructions such as 'use a subagent to verify', because the model already verifies its own work. The model-specific advice differs, so put review at milestone boundaries rather than at every step (inference). The owner's template already uses a fresh agent to review the full diff and a separate agent to disprove findings.
findings.implication: At the end of each milestone, not each step, a fresh subagent reviews the milestone diff against PLAN.md and features.json. It reports only gaps that affect rules fidelity, correctness, or a stated requirement. Fix those, or list them in progress.md with a reason. Do not add other double-check steps.

findings.topic: Prevent early stopping without removing the owner's checkpoints
findings.claim: Current models can end a turn by announcing the next step instead of doing it, can stop because they worry about context, or can ask permission for work already requested. The docs give prompt text for each case and recommend naming the pauses you do want.
findings.detail: The platform docs suggest telling the model that context compacts automatically, so it should not stop early. Prompting Claude Fable 5.1 ('Finish the whole task') and Opus 5.5 ('Unattended agentic runs') give instructions against ending on a plan or a promise. Fable 5 suggests pausing only for destructive actions, real scope changes, or input only the user can give. Rajasekaran 2026 found 'context anxiety' strong on Sonnet 4.5 and largely gone on Opus 4.5. The owner's template already says to batch questions in one message and keep working meanwhile.
findings.implication: Your context compacts automatically. Do not stop, summarize, or suggest a new session because of context length; update progress.md and continue. Do not end a turn with a plan or a promise; do the step. Stop only for the items under 'Stop and ask me before'. Batch those questions in one message and keep working on everything that does not depend on them.

findings.topic: Tell compaction what to keep
findings.claim: Compaction summaries keep more of what matters when told explicitly what to preserve. Claude Code supports a CLAUDE.md instruction for this.
findings.detail: Claude Code best practices suggest a CLAUDE.md line such as one that always preserves the modified-file list and the test commands. Prompting Claude Fable 5.1 gives a six-item summary instruction: problems and how they were resolved, approaches tried or set aside, decisions and constraints stated exactly, current status, open items, and exact identifiers and numbers.
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1 (section 'Tell the model what to preserve in compaction summaries')
findings.implication: Add to CLAUDE.md: 'When compacting during engine work, keep the current feature id, files changed, the exact test and match commands with seeds, the last bench number, open failures with seeds, and every decision I made, word for word.'

findings.topic: Keep CLAUDE.md short and concrete
findings.claim: Long or vague instruction files reduce adherence. The docs set a target of under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md, ask for instructions concrete enough to verify, and warn that heavy emphasis and conflicting rules both weaken compliance.
findings.detail: The memory docs: target under 200 lines; imports do not reduce context cost; if two instructions conflict, Claude may pick either. Best practices: for each line, ask whether removing it would cause mistakes; add IMPORTANT to at most one line; use skills for knowledge needed only sometimes. A secondary summary of OpenAI's essay reports that one large AGENTS.md failed and that a short map pointing into versioned docs worked; the primary essay returned HTTP 403. Capi's CLAUDE.md is currently 30 lines.
findings.implication: Add at most five lines to CLAUDE.md for the engine: where the state files are, the engine check, bench, and match commands, and the compaction line. Everything else goes in docs/engine/PLAN.md. Write each rule as a concrete check, for example 'run npm run engine:check before every commit', not 'test your changes'.

findings.topic: Plain imperatives with reasons, not shouting
findings.claim: Current Claude models follow system prompts closely and overreact to aggressive emphasis. The docs recommend normal wording and a short reason for each instruction, so the model can generalize from it.
findings.detail: The platform docs say Opus 4.5 and 4.6 can overtrigger on prompts written for older models, and recommend replacing 'CRITICAL: You MUST' with plain wording. They also show that giving the reason behind an instruction improves results. Fable 5 notes that brief instructions now steer behavior without listing every case. Anthropic's 2025 quickstart prompts use all-caps warnings, which is older practice. The owner's template already uses plain imperatives with short inline reasons.
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices (sections 'Add context to improve performance', 'Tool usage', 'Migration considerations')
findings.implication: Write every rule as a plain imperative with a one-clause reason when the reason is not obvious, as in 'Keep the anon-key fallback, since production needs it until I deploy the service role key.' Do not use capitals, CRITICAL, or MUST.

findings.topic: Scope control and layered build
findings.claim: Opus-class and Fable models tend to add unrequested features, abstractions, defensive code, and extra tests. The docs give scope-limiting instructions. The owner's code philosophy requires the same thing: the simplest working version first, then layers.
findings.detail: The platform docs' 'Overeagerness' sample, Fable 5's 'Consider all effort levels' sample (which also bans feature flags and compatibility shims), and Fable 5.1's 'Keep changes and tests to what the task asks for' sample all ask for minimal changes and for follow-ups to be reported instead of done. The owner's global CLAUDE.md says: simplest implementation that fully meets the current requirement; build in layers; no backward-compatibility layers; check existing dependencies first. Rajasekaran 2026 found the opposite risk too: without a planner, the generator scoped too little. So the first session should expand the full feature list, and later sessions should stay inside it (inference).
sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1 (section 'Keep changes and tests to what the task asks for')
findings.implication: Build in layers. First get the smallest engine that works end to end: legal moves from packages/engine, a random and a greedy baseline, and a match runner. Add search, inference over hidden hands, evaluation, and analysis on top of that running product. Build only what the current milestone needs. Report any other bug or improvement you notice as a follow-up in progress.md instead of doing it. No speculative options, flags, or compatibility shims.

findings.topic: What subagents see, and restating rules to them
findings.claim: Subagents start with a fresh context. They load the CLAUDE.md hierarchy but not the conversation, the pasted prompt, or invoked skills. Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md entirely. Rules that live only in the build prompt must be restated when delegating.
findings.detail: The Claude Code subagent docs say the main conversation still has its rules when it reads a subagent's results, so a rule that must reach the subagent should be restated in the delegation prompt. By default, 20 subagents can run at once and nesting goes three levels deep (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS, CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH). Prompting Claude Opus 5 recommends limiting delegation to large, independent tasks.
sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md (sections on startup context and limits, fetched 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: When you delegate, put the hard constraints that apply into the delegation prompt: packages/engine is the spec and stays unchanged, no dependency changes, no em dashes, the evidence rules. Explore agents do not see CLAUDE.md. Delegate only large independent work, such as a literature survey or a separate experiment; do core search and rules work in the main session.

findings.topic: Use ultracode and workflows for fan-out phases, background shells for long jobs
findings.claim: The owner's template starts with the keyword ultracode, which makes Claude write a dynamic workflow script. Workflows suit audits, cross-checked research, and fix-until-green loops. They cannot take user input mid-run, and they resume only within the same session.
findings.detail: The workflows docs: the keyword works only in a prompt the user types, not with -p or in scheduled tasks. Workflows run up to 16 agents at once by default and up to 1,000 agents per run. A 'Large workflow' warning appears above 25 agents or a projected 1.5 million tokens. Runs are resumable within the same session. Sign-off between stages needs a separate workflow per stage. The owner's template keeps xcodebuild and EAS builds in the main session's background shell, never in a subagent, and his memory lists 'agent-killed builds' as a known dev-loop problem. Long engine matches look similar (inference).
sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows.md (sections 'Where the keyword works', 'Behavior and limits', 'Cost', fetched 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: Keep ultracode at the top only if the first session's survey and the milestone reviews should run as workflows. Run long match and tuning jobs from the main session's background shell with logs on disk, never inside a subagent, and read the summary line when they finish.

findings.topic: Parallel agents only on independent work
findings.claim: On one tightly coupled task, parallel agents hit the same bug and overwrite each other's fixes. Flat coordination through locks collapses throughput and makes agents risk-averse. Parallelism pays off only when tasks are truly separate.
findings.detail: Carlini 2026: on the Linux kernel, all 16 agents hit the same bug and overwrote each other, so 16 agents gave no speedup until the GCC-oracle split. Agents also often broke existing features, which led to a stricter CI gate. Cursor (Lin, 2026-01-14): 20 agents coordinating through a lock file slowed to the throughput of 2 or 3. Without hierarchy, agents avoided hard tasks and made small safe changes. Cursor says periodic fresh starts are still needed against drift. A promotional single-project post (battyterm 2026) reports 5 agents slower than 3 (about 22 vs 18 minutes) and bugs found only at module integration: a perft count of 19 instead of 20, and mismatched evaluation scales.
findings.implication: Build the rules adapter, search, and evaluation sequentially in one session. Run in parallel only independent jobs, such as separate match runs, separate evaluation experiments on their own branches or worktrees, or literature reading. Each parallel job reports a summary with evidence; the main session integrates and reruns the differential suite and bench.

findings.topic: Write the prompt at the right altitude: goals, constraints, checks
findings.claim: Each harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do. Prompts should state the goal, the constraints, and the checks, and leave the method open where the model is capable. Over-scripted prompts written for older models can lower quality.
findings.detail: Rajasekaran 2026 removed sprints and per-sprint evaluation for Opus 4.6, kept the planner, and advises removing one component at a time and measuring. Rajasekaran et al. 2025 describe the right altitude as between brittle if-else logic and vague guidance. Fable 5 notes that skills written for earlier models are often too prescriptive. Cursor 2026 states that prompts mattered more than the harness or the model.
findings.implication: Name the target capabilities, the hard constraints, and the measurement protocol exactly. Do not prescribe the search algorithm or architecture as fixed steps. Say: 'Choose the method from the research in docs/engine/research/, record why in PLAN.md, and change it if the match results say so.'

findings.topic: Originality and licensing of borrowed engine code
findings.claim: An agent-built engine drew community scrutiny when AGPL-licensed code was found in it, and the project then adopted strict rules: take ideas from other engines, never their expression. Capi's repo is public and has no license file, so borrowed code would raise license questions the owner must decide.
findings.detail: Coda's README describes an audit after community feedback reported AGPL code, plus an early license mislabel. Its CLAUDE.md forbids carrying over foreign constants, code, or file:line citations, requires closing the reference before writing, and requires deleting and rebuilding a contaminated branch instead of amending it. Observed read-only: /Users/Adelson/Desktop/personal/capi has no LICENSE file and package.json has no license field. The owner's template already forbids dependency changes without asking.
sources: https://github.com/adamtwiss/coda (README and CLAUDE.md section 'Originality and licensing', fetched 2026-10-25)
findings.implication: Read other engines and papers for ideas only. Do not copy code, constants, or data from other projects into Capi, and cite papers at the idea level in comments. Adding a dependency, vendoring code, or choosing a license needs my approval first.

findings.topic: Large agent builds that shipped broken, and agent-written tests that prove too little
findings.claim: High-profile autonomous builds produced large codebases whose CI failed or which needed human cleanup. Practitioners point out that trusting tests the agent wrote itself is not enough to verify behavior.
findings.detail: The Register (2026-01-22) reports that Cursor's FastRender browser (about one week, self-described as about three million lines) had a CI job failure rate reported at 88 percent. Some developers compiled it only after fixes. Böckeler (martinfowler.com, 2026-04-02) calls functional behavior 'the elephant in the room' and says checking AI-generated tests is not yet good enough. Rajasekaran 2026 found features that looked complete but were stubs (clips could not be dragged; audio recording was stub-only).
findings.implication: The owner-defined oracles are the acceptance tests: packages/engine for rules, the match protocol in this prompt for strength, and the running app for bots and analysis. The agent may add its own tests, but those tests never count as acceptance on their own. No stubs: a feature marked passing works end to end through its verify command.

findings.topic: Owner template structure (polish-pass-1.1.md)
findings.claim: The template is 76 lines, 1,496 words, and contains no em dashes. It has a header, a paste instruction, and eight sections marked by plain-text labels (not Markdown headers), in a fixed order.
findings.detail: Lines 1-5: '# Prompt: <title>', one sentence ('Paste everything below the line into a fresh Claude Code session opened in this repo.'), then a horizontal rule. Line 7: the keyword ultracode on its own line. Goal (9-10): one paragraph of four sentences: what to do, the order of judgment (player first, then risk), and the action sequence ending in the final deliverable. Context (12-17): bullets of facts: build state, scope boundary, what a deploy affects, a 'Read first' list of exact files including absolute memory-file paths with the reason they are needed, and work the owner may do meanwhile with a stop trigger. Hard constraints (19-30): numbered 1-11, one rule each, with exact identifiers (commit hashes, file paths, version pins), allowed and forbidden actions, an owner-only console boundary, a style rule, and a commit rule. Method (32-38): numbered phases: baseline gates and parallel mapping that changes nothing; use the product as a first-time user; audit in independent dimensions, one agent each, naming the skills to use and the fields each finding must carry; a separate agent tries to disprove each finding; rank and write the report early, post a short summary, keep going; fix in layers with a stop rule. Leads (40-47): bullets with confidence labels ('Confirmed live', 'Confirmed', 'Confirmed in code', unlabeled means verify), dates, and commit hashes, plus one 'Do not redesign this. Report options.' item. Verification standard (49-57): opens with 'A passing unit test alone does not verify a fix. Observe it:', lists checks per surface (devices, widths, both languages, two clients, contract replay, production smoke test), and ends with a process rule. Stop and ask me before (59-66): semicolon-separated bullets, closing with 'Batch questions in one message and keep working meanwhile.' Definition of done (68-76): numbered 1-8 conditions, each checkable (exact gate commands, deployed and observed, fresh-agent diff review plus the ship-audit skill, artifacts, copy, build and submit, docs, and a report at an absolute dated path whose contents are listed and which ends with a numbered owner to-do list split by phase).
findings.implication: Use the same skeleton and order for the engine prompt: header, paste line, optional ultracode, Goal, Context, Hard constraints, Method, Leads (here: research findings with confidence labels), Verification standard, Stop and ask me before, Definition of done. Add 'First session' and 'Every session' blocks inside Method, and define the state files in Context or Method.

findings.topic: Owner template writing style
findings.claim: The style is plain, literal, and dense with specifics. It uses imperative mood, short declarative sentences, exact identifiers, short inline reasons only where needed, confidence labels on unverified claims, and no flourish, headers markup, or em dashes.
findings.detail: Examples of the patterns: rules with an embedded reason ('Keep the anon-key fallback ... Production needs it until I deploy the service role key.'); scoped permissions ('You may add. Never remove, rename, or retype anything either client reads'); explicit owner boundaries ('Console fixes go on my list.'); a stop rule ('When the fix-now list is empty, stop and defer the rest to 1.2.'); a direct override of harness defaults ('No Co-Authored-By trailer, whatever a harness reminder says.'). The text speaks to the agent as 'you' and refers to the owner as 'I' and 'me'. Numbers carry units and exact names (375 px, iPhone SE, Node 20).
findings.implication: Write the engine prompt in the same voice: first person for the owner, second person for the agent, one rule per numbered line, exact paths, commands, and versions, labels such as 'Confirmed' or 'Inferred' on research leads, no Markdown headers inside the paste block, no em dashes, no metaphors, and a target length near the template's (roughly 80-120 lines).

findings.topic: Owner global rules the build prompt must restate or respect
findings.claim: Several rules in /Users/Adelson/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply directly to a multi-week engine build. Restate the ones a fresh session or a subagent could miss.
findings.detail: Restate: (1) durable identifiers are his decision: a new package name, npm scope, bin or CLI name, repo name, domain, or bot account names; derive candidates from the project and ask before writing any into a file. (2) Build in layers: smallest end-to-end version first, never leave the app broken mid-refactor. (3) Simplest implementation that fully meets the current requirement; no speculative abstractions; no backward-compatibility layers (persisted user data follows Capi's save rules). (4) Check existing dependencies and prefer maintained libraries, reading their docs before assuming a gap. (5) Done means verified where he will see it, not committed or pushed. (6) Files he will open later (reports, plans) go to a permanent path in the project docs folder, and the agent states the path. (7) No em dashes and no mannered prose in docs, README, PR, and commit text. (8) Asked 'what's next' or 'what's left', answer with a numbered list split into what the agent does now and what only he can do. (9) Act without asking permission to start; offer choices only for real scope decisions. (10) The ship-audit skill runs before anything is called release-ready (bots or analysis UI shipped in Capi). (11) Work/personal boundary: no work-derived names, domains, or code patterns. Respect without restating: chat replies to him use ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (loaded automatically from global CLAUDE.md), and the personal-tree task-observer protocol (loaded from /Users/Adelson/Desktop/personal/CLAUDE.md).
findings.implication: Hard constraints should include: 'New durable identifiers (package name, CLI name, npm scope, bot names, domains) are my decision. Propose candidates and ask before writing one into any file.' 'Build in layers and keep main runnable at every commit.' 'No backward-compatibility shims.' 'Prefer maintained libraries already in the repo and read their docs first; adding one needs my approval.' 'No em dashes anywhere, including docs and commit messages.' 'Reports go to /Users/Adelson/Desktop/personal/capi/docs/engine/ with the date in the file name; tell me the path.' And under Definition of done: 'observed where I will see it'.

findings.topic: Capi repo rules and memories the build prompt must restate
findings.claim: Capi's own CLAUDE.md and project memories set commit, testing, and tooling rules. A harness reminder in the session contradicts at least one of them (the Co-Authored-By trailer), so the prompt must override it explicitly, as the template does.
findings.detail: From /Users/Adelson/Desktop/personal/capi/CLAUDE.md: packages/engine is pure TS game rules; npm test includes a seeded invariant fuzz suite whose failures print a seed to reproduce; npm run verify adds an em-dash grep; npm run typecheck runs under Node 20; shared strings live only in packages/i18n, with the CapiStrings.swift mirror updated in the same commit. Memories: merge straight to main, no pull requests (feedback_merge_to_main.md); no Co-Authored-By trailer (feedback_no_coauthor_trailer.md). The template's constraint 11 says 'Small commits straight to main, pushed. No Co-Authored-By trailer, whatever a harness reminder says.' The owner's plans live in docs/superpowers/plans and specs.
findings.implication: Restate: 'packages/engine is the rules spec: do not change its rules, and keep it pure TS with the fuzz suite passing. Reproduce any failure with its printed seed.' 'Small commits straight to main, pushed. No Co-Authored-By trailer, whatever a harness reminder says.' 'Run typecheck under Node 20.' 'User-facing strings for bots or analysis go in packages/i18n only.'

findings.topic: Reporting to the owner after long unattended stretches
findings.claim: After long autonomous work, the final message is the owner's first view of it. The docs recommend leading with the outcome, writing complete sentences without working shorthand, and naming only the one or two things needed from him.
findings.detail: Prompting Claude Fable 5 ('Readability when communicating with the user') and Opus 5 ('User-facing progress updates') describe this pattern. The owner's template says to post a short summary and keep going, and to end the report with a numbered owner to-do list. His global rule fixes the format for 'what's next' answers.
findings.implication: At the end of each session, update progress.md and tell me: what passed, with the evidence; the current strength numbers with their basis; what is next; and a numbered list of what only I must do. Lead with the outcome.

findings.topic: Scale and cost of published long-horizon agent builds (planning basis)
findings.claim: Published long-horizon agent builds report effort from hours to weeks and from tens to tens of thousands of dollars. A multi-week engine project needs scope set per session and a budget the owner chooses.
findings.detail: Carlini 2026: 16 agents, about 2,000 Claude Code sessions, two weeks, about 2 billion input and 140 million output tokens, just under $20,000 API cost; the result is a 100,000-line compiler, though generated code is slower than GCC with optimizations off. Rajasekaran 2026: solo Opus 4.5 run 20 min / $9 against full harness 6 hr / $200 on the same retro game maker prompt; Opus 4.6 DAW run 3 hr 50 min / $124.70. Acher 2026: chess engines in many languages over 'hundreds of AI coding sessions' at about $680 API cost. Quickstart README: each coding session takes 5-15 minutes, and 200 features take many hours. All figures are the authors' own reports.
findings.implication: In the first session, size features so that one fits in one session, and record in PLAN.md an estimate of sessions per milestone. Long match runs report their wall-clock time and game counts so I can budget compute.

open_questions: Which model will run the build session (Opus 5.5 at default medium effort, or Fable 5.1)? The model docs disagree on explicit verification instructions: the Opus 5 page says to remove 'use a subagent to verify' lines, and the Fable 5 page says to add regular fresh-context verifier checks. The final wording of the review step depends on the model.

The new engine package name, any CLI or bin name, bot account names, and any domain for an analysis tool are durable identifiers. The owner must choose them, or approve candidates, before the prompt names them.
Should the build enforce its gates with a Stop hook or a /goal condition in .claude/settings.json? That is persistent configuration, so the owner must approve it.
Where will long match and tuning runs execute (the owner's Mac or cloud), and what compute and API budget per week is acceptable? This sets game counts and SPRT bounds.
